speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a brief report about a trip which has necessitated my absence during the past two weeks. During these two weeks I have, as the house already knows, attended the commonwealth economic conference at Accra with my colleague the Minister of Finance, and later visited our trade commissioners in five of the important markets of Europe.
At the Accra conference I outlined the importance to Canada of maintaining the commonwealth trading arrangements which have been so beneficial to our farmers, fishermen, lumbermen, miners, other primary producers and manufacturers in the United Kingdom market, and also to United Kingdom producers selling in the Canadian market. I pointed out that acceptance of the common market tariff by the United Kingdom would mean for us the loss of free entry for a number of important industrial raw materials, the whole range of semi-processed and manufactured goods, and most of our agricultural exports.
I told the meeting that out of total sales to the United Kingdom last year amounting to $915 million some $691 million, or 76 per cent, would be affected by United Kingdom acceptance of the common market tariff; $631 million would in our view be seriously affected; $584 million of this trade would be faced with higher tariffs, and $553 million would be faced with not only a loss of preference but, in most cases, a preference against Canadians and in favour of Europeans. I said this would be an entirely new and disturbing situation for us. I pointed out that such figures are by no means a full measure of the potential damage of such a move for Canada. In some cases the loss of preference, let alone reverse preference, could eliminate Canadians from the United Kingdom market.
The other commonwealth delegations attending the conference expressed similar concern over the effect which the loss of present trading arrangements in the United Kingdom
8900	HOUSE OF
Commonwealth Economic Conference market would have on their economies, and the communique, which was adopted unanimously, expresses accurately the grave concern felt by members of the commonwealth about this matter.
At no time did I say anything which could be construed as an ultimatum to the United Kingdom government that she must choose between the European common market and the commonwealth. I endeavoured to point out to the United Kingdom government the importance to Canadian producers of maintaining our present trading arrangements in the United Kingdom market, and the damage that will result if these trading arrangements are not maintained. I pointed out that our economy would be harmed to the degree that the United Kingdom government is unable to maintain these trading arrangements.
I think the house might be interested to learn of the increase in exports between this country and the United Kingdom which has developed since this government took office. In 1956 Canadian exports to the United Kingdom market amounted to $812,668,049. Last year exports to the United Kingdom market from Canada amounted to $915,289,654. Our exports to all commonwealth countries, including the United Kingdom, in 1956 amounted to $1,055,833,671. Last year they amounted to $1,244,519,631.1 cite these figures simply to show how trade with the United Kingdom and the commonwealth as a whole has been increasing during the time we have been in office, and the importance of this trade to Canada.
After leaving Ghana I visited our trade commissioners in Italy, West Germany, France, Belgium and the United Kingdom. My purpose in doing so was threefold. First of all I wanted to examine the opportunities which exist for expanding trade in those countries. Having discussed this matter with our trade commissioners and with businessmen, I am convinced that we can substantially expand our trade in those markets if our businessmen will visit the markets and show prospective customers good samples at competitive prices. Canadians have a lot of goodwill in Europe and people there are anxious to do business with us, but they want to meet our salesmen face to face and discuss prospective sales with them.
My second purpose was to find out at first hand if our posts abroad are carrying out efficiently the task I have given them of making it as easy for a Canadian businessman to sell his products in the country in which they are serving as it is for him to do business in Canada. I find that this is being done very effectively in the five countries which I visited.


My third purpose was to find out if the department in Ottawa can do a better job of backing up our trade commissioners in the important tasks they have been given to do. A number of good suggestions were made to me and these will be put into effect in the near future.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I felt that the visits I made to posts abroad were very useful indeed, and I intend to make similar visits to other posts abroad just as soon as sufficient time is available.

subtopic: DISARMAMENT-STATEMENT ON CANADIAN POSITION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: DISARMAMENT-STATEMENT ON CANADIAN POSITION
speechtext:
Yesterday President Kennedy, in his speech to the United Nations general assembly, revealed new disarmament proposals. The new plan has been submitted to the United Nations in a United States document. I want to make clear at once that it has full Canadian support, and that Canada took an active part in the preparation of these proposals. I think the house might be interested in a statement on their main features.
Throughout the summer we have been working closely with representatives of the other members of the ten nation disarmament committee to get these new proposals ready. There has been very full consultation with other members of the western alliance. The Canadian point of view was presented, and vigorously presented, in the course of those meetings, and the majority of the suggestions made by Canada are embodied in the new plan as enunciated.
These proposals meet the wishes of the average person throughout the world for a really significant measure of disarmament to be attained at the earliest possible date. As well, they underline the necessity of viewing disarmament as an uninterrupted process directed toward a definite goal.
These are factors to which great importance was attached by the commonwealth prime ministers at the meeting earlier this year. It is significant that they now find a place in the new disarmament proposals. In point of fact, the communique issued by the prime ministers' conference represented, I think, the first occasion on which all of the nations of the commonwealth joined together in one proposal and in one compendium of suggestions on this or any other matter.
The new plan, as enunciated, does not stop at pious deference to the ultimate goal of general disarmament. It provides an opportunity for undertaking immediate measures

to put a stop to the arms race, to reduce the dangers of surprise attack and reverse the frightening spiral of threats to peace which now confronts the world. It is clear proof of the fact that the western nations are not out to promote empty slogans but are sincerely desirous of seeking active, concrete disarmament as soon as possible.
The most striking point of the new plan is that it provides for a large measure of disarmament at the very first stage. It would get disarmament started right away in all important areas. In that regard, I should point out that there are substantial proposals to deal with the most dangerous of modern armaments, nuclear weapons, and the means for their delivery. The production of nuclear weapons material is to be stopped at the very outset. Quantities of fissionable material from past production for military purposes are to be transferred to peaceful uses. In that connection I might point out that when I spoke at the United Nations assembly in September, 1960, that was one of the matters advanced.
In conjunction with these measures, provision is also made to stop the further spread of nuclear weapons by prohibiting any country which possesses them from relinquishing their control to countries which do not. The section in question, to which I might refer, reads as follows:
States owning nuclear weapons shall not relinquish control of such weapons to any nation not owning them and shall not transmit to any such nation the information or material necessary for their manufacture. States not owning nuclear weapons shall not manufacture such weapons, attempt to obtain control of such weapons belonging to other states, or seek to receive information or material necessary to their manufacture.
There is also provision at the beginning of the program for the reduction of existing stocks of the major means of directing nuclear weapons to their targets, "strategic delivery vehicles" as they are called in the plan. The production and testing of specified types of these weapons are also to be limited or discontinued altogether. This provision, too, was one of those I placed before the assembly in September, 1960, when I pointed out the need of a law for outer space before the dangerous potentialities of the future would permit of the launching of war as against all mankind from outer space; and that outer space should be available to all nations, great or small, in an equal manner and should be used for peaceful purposes.
These measures suggested by the President go a long way toward removing the widespread fear that the nuclear powers are embarked on a contest which they cannot stop and which no one can win. Their importance cannot be exaggerated.

I think it is apparent that while nuclear weapons present the most frightening threat of modern times, the so-called conventional means of warfare can also cause-and have done so on more than one occasion in our lifetime-extraordinary devastation and misery.
There are provisions for significant manpower reductions, to 2.1 million men in the case of the United States and the Soviet union in the first stage. It is also provided that conventional armaments will be reduced. Further, the plan calls for limitations on the production of certain categories of conventional weapons.
There are measures designed to reduce the dangers of surprise attack or accidental war through advance notification of military manoeuvres and ground observation posts. An international commission is to be established to study further measures of this kind. The importance of these provisions is apparent in a world where a miscalculation could result in all-out war before either side has had time for second thought, sober second thought, on the subject.
A further section of the plan deals with the peaceful usage of outer space. I have already made reference to that. The plan would prohibit the stationing in outer space of weapons of mass destruction, and calls for a system of advance notification of satellite launchings so that all states will be reassured that these launchings are peaceful in intent. The Secretary of State for External Affairs on more than one occasion has advanced this and other suggestions that now find their way into the presentation of this plan.
The entire plan is to be implemented under the strictest international verification. The provisions for effective control are among the most important, because they give the assurance that is sought by all that the measures undertaken will in fact be carried out, and that all states will fully respect their obligations.
Finally, there are significant new provisions for increasing the strength and effectiveness of international machinery to keep the peace. These proposals are given prominence because it is clear that no states will be prepared to sacrifice the means by which they now provide self defence, unless there is sufficient guarantee that there will be effective arrangements by which the security of all states can be protected internationally. The new proposals look to the development of existing United Nations arrangements for keeping the peace, and call for the creation of a United Nations peace observation group which could investigate any incident anywhere in the world which would be likely to constitute a threat to the peace. In addition
Canadian Disarmament Position -and this has been the hope for 1,000 years -the creation of a genuine international force, to take place in the second stage of disarmament.
All these things constitute a broad program the goal of which is to remove all threat of war and to ensure that disputes between nations will be settled by peaceful means. After further development in stages two and three, if the plan is accepted, the only armaments and armed forces which would be retained would be those required to protect the security of individual citizens and for contributions as well to an international peace force.
I think the proposals are impressive and that, if they were accepted, they would bring about a major achievement in the field of disarmament effectively and quickly. To what extent they will prove acceptable to the Soviet union will be seen only in detailed negotiations. I think the proposals are realistic. While all of us feel a sense of encouragement with every indication of even the slightest change, I think the acceptance by the United States and the U.S.S.R. of the basic principles which underlie and guide these negotiations will be a step forward.
There are other problems which remain to be resolved. An element of co-operation on both sides can still contribute to their solution at an early date. It is an overriding obligation for everyone in our country as well as throughout the nations of the world to ensure that this challenge shall be met without further delay.
In the midst of the difficulties of the present, the fears that overhang all mankind, the proposals constitute great hope if accepted; for if the expenditures now being made in the field of armament could be applied to those talks that raise the living standards of men, we would be entering a new era in which the past would be far exceeded by the potentialities which technology permits and allows in the present.

Canadian Disarmament Position stopping the further spread of nuclear weapons. Last year at the general assembly the Canadian representative said this:
... we believe that the spread of nuclear weapons to an ever increasing number of countries would pose a threat to mankind. We consider that the only satisfactory way to dispel the dangers inherent in this possibility is through international agreement on a comprehensive and carefully verified system of disarmament.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement of the Prime Minister was something of a general summary of the speech of the President of the United States at the United Nations. I think peace loving people throughout the world will in general welcome the tone as well as most of the content of the speech delivered by President Kennedy. In the last few weeks, without wise counsel from important leaders of the world, the world was hell bent toward nuclear war. I think the statement of President Kennedy may bring to the councils of the world a measure of sense.
The resumption by the U.S.S.R. of nuclear tests was perhaps the greatest single blow in recent weeks to the hopes of mankind for an enduring peace. We have criticized the United States for resuming nuclear tests, but we welcome the statement of President Kennedy that cessation of nuclear tests by all nations should be agreed upon forthwith.
We welcome the statement by the Prime Minister that Canada had been consulted before these proposals were put forward by President Kennedy. It seems to me that President Kennedy, in stating that there should be no further extension of control of nuclear weapons, strengthens the opinion of those Canadians who believe that Canada should not accept nuclear weapons. We do not feel that nuclear weapons should be on Canadian soil, whether or not those weapons are under the control of Canada itself.
In recent weeks so much of the talk has been about preparation for eventual war that it seems a very satisfactory thing to hear the leader of the United States talk about peace and the terrible results of an atomic war. The world is looking to the United Nations now for leadership in the field of peace. We hope that the United Nations, as requested by President Kennedy, Canada and other nations, will appoint a secretary general who can continue the good work of the late Dag Hammarskj old.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Monday, September 25, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-126 respecting the construction of a line of railway in the province of Alberta and in the Northwest Territories by Canadian National Railway Company from a point at or near Grimshaw, in the province of Alberta, in a northerly direction to Great Slave lake, in the Northwest Territories-Mr. Balcer- Mr. Chown in the chair.
On clause 6-Agreement required.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
When we adjourned last evening I had just asked the minister for certain information and he had undertaken to provide that information if possible. I am glad the Minister of Finance is here this morning, and perhaps I could have his attention; because if the Minister of Transport cannot provide this information I am perfectly sure the Minister of Finance can. Perhaps I should recall what it was I said:
I believe we ought to have an indication other than merely the minister's expression of confidence that traffic will be available in approximately that volume. I do not necessarily refer to traffic in concentrates, but to lumber and any other commodities that might be shipped. This railway will not carry passengers, nor will it carry much package freight in an area where there is already a highway, as anyone who has had much experience of highways and railways knows. It is likely that this railway will carry only bulk cargo of one kind or another. I believe we ought to have a much harder estimate. When we resume in committee tomorrow the minister should tell us what the estimate of the cost to the treasury is based upon, including the projected rate of interest they are working on.
By the cost to the treasury I do not mean the $86 million; I mean the cost of carrying

that $86 million over the period, since there is no provision in the agreement for any direct return on it.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: As I explained yesterday, this money will be paid to the company out of the consolidated revenue fund from time to time under the direction of the governor in council and upon a report of the Minister of Transport concerning the mileage of railway line constructed or to be constructed, in such amounts and in such manners and subject to such conditions, if any, as the governor in council deems expedient. There will be the same conditions, the same charges, as those applied in respect of any other subsidies paid out of consolidated revenue for any special purpose.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: I am sure the Minister of Finance would not have agreed to this agreement and to the introduction of this bill without having a projection over the period until 1966-during which the railway is not going to be operating, according to the prospects-[DOT] of what this is going to cost the treasury. I am not talking about the $86 million itself. I am talking about the carrying charges on that sum as the money is borrowed over that period. I think before we approve this bill we ought to know what the estimate is. I realize that the actual amount will depend on how quickly the railway is built. The slower it is built the more it is going to cost, because more money will have to be provided for a longer period. I think the Minister of Finance, as the custodian of the treasury, should tell us what estimate has been made of the carrying charges up to the time the railway begins to operate in 1966.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: I think anybody will realize that if this money is to be borrowed we shall have to pay the interest in the bond market of Canada at that time. We do not know what this is going to be three years from now, for example, or at any given time. It will be whatever the market will require at that time.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: May I ask the Minister of Finance what is the rate of interest which is being paid by the government now on short term borrowings?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
It depends entirely on the maturity. The treasury bill rate has been remarkably low for some time now. Our own market borrowings have been in the short term field in keeping with the policy which I announced in the budget. We have not been borrowing in the long end of the market for some time. I shall be pleased, when we come
Canadian National Railways to the discussion of my estimates, to deal with the question of interest rates if the hon. member wishes.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: Can the minister not give some indication of what rate the government would have to pay if, say, $100 million were required?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: That would depend on the time of the borrowing; it would depend on conditions at the time. It would depend on the maturity date, and on many other factors.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: I asked the minister to tell us as of now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: I said that we have not been borrowing on the long end of the market for some time for the reasons I indicated in the budget speech. We have been leaving that end of the market open to the provinces and the municipalities. The maturity would be a matter for decision when the time came. I think the hon. member will not overlook the fact that this money is not all required at one particular time; it would be a matter of taking care of this additional requirement along with all the other cash requirements of the government.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
I realize that, and if the minister had been here last night-he was not here, through no fault of his own-he would be aware that the discussion had to do with regular amounts which would have to be provided year by year until the railway was built.
I come back to the question I asked the minister last night in connection with the amount of concentrates required by the Northern Alberta Railways to amortize the capital over a period of years. The minister said he would consult with his officers to ascertain whether there had been an amount of concentrates per year required by the N.A.R. in case they should decide to build this line with their own capital.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
I understood from the discussion last night that this information was not required any longer. The hon. member for Laurier himself gave the figure; he had made the calculation. We had a rate for 215,000 tons of concentrates and he made the calculation himself based upon that figure and gave the results to the committee. I thought he was satisfied with that. If I understand him well, he wants to know what the Northern Alberta Railways figured would be the full requirement of concentrates which should be shipped on that line so as to completely amortize the total cost of the line. I am sorry, but I have not got that figure at the present time. My people can endeavour to get it, though I am not sure whether we

Canadian National Railways have in the department any figure prepared by the Northern Alberta Railway Company with regard to such a requirement.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
I put the question to the minister, as reported at page 8896 of Hansard, as follows:
Would it not then require, to amortize everything, something in the neighbourhood of 800,000 or 900,000 tons of concentrates per year over a period of 25 years, not 10 years?
The minister replied:
Tha is quite possible. I know that the economists in my department have worked out all these figures, but I have not got them with me. I do not disagree with the hon. member, but what I wish to say is that this line is not being built exclusively for one mine.
Later on, as reported at page 8897, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said:
In a qualified way the minister assented to the proposition advanced by the hon. member for Laurier that it would be 800,000 or 900,000 tons instead of the 215,000, which is over four times what they are being asked for over a period of years.
I cannot readily locate it in Hansard, but I understood the minister to say that he would check with his officers to find out whether that was correct. The minister now says he could obtain those figures at a later date. I would appreciate it if he would secure them before the conclusion of this discussion.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: I have just received information from my officials. If all the traffic from Pine Point were to consist of concentrates a volume of approximately 800,000 tons would be required to amortize the capital cost. What the hon. member for Laurier seems to forget is that there would be concentrates other than from Pine Point. This does not take into account the traffic moving into Pine Point mines including equipment, supplies and other things, nor does it take into account commercial fishing at Great Slave lake which will be transported on this line, together with other commodities such as lumber and agricultural produce.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: Does the note which the minister received say anything about the length of time required? The minister will remember that the agreement extends for only ten years. My suggestion was that when worked out mathematically it would take between 800,000 and 900,000 tons over a period of 25 years. That is four times greater so far as the volume is concerned, and two and a half times greater so far as the time is concerned. Has the minister any information as to the length of the term of the agreement?

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
I agree with my hon. friend that approximately 800,000 or 900,000 tons

will be required over a period of 25 years if we ship on that line exclusively concentrates from Pine Point.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
That is fine. I thank the minister. I did not hear him refer to the period of 25 years.
I wish now to follow up another point raised by my friend the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate in connection with the demand for concentrates over the period of time mentioned in the agreement. Mr. D. F. Purves who appeared as a witness before the standing committee on Thursday, September 21, 1961, as reported at page 258 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence, when referring to the assurance of a continuing market for concentrates, said:
We do not have any assurance in that regard, but we do have the other assurance with which we primarily are concerned. That is, the company will ship 215,000 tons per year or pay a penalty.
The question that arises is this. Did the government make any survey of the future of these concentrates? From the evidence it would appear that both the C.N.R. and the government took the position of saying that they did not have to worry about that because that is the problem of Cominco, and that if they were willing to enter into an agreement that was no concern of the government or the C.N.R. That is the impression I received from the testimony of the witness, Mr. Purves, and also from what the minister said.
As the committee knows, there is a drive on in the United States congress to raise tariffs and also to impose quotas upon lead and zinc. The question that comes to mind is this. Suppose the decision with respect to lead and zinc is similar to that in relation to uranium. What steps has the government taken, either through an analysis by an interdepartmental committee or a study made by its economists and experts, to ascertain the future of lead and zinc tariffs? This is not a matter involving a few million dollars but perhaps $100 million. I wish to be enlightened on that point if the minister is able to assist me.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
The experts and economists in my department who dealt with this agreement reached the conclusion that the special guarantee from Pine Point and Cominco of a shipment of 215,000 tons a year for a period of ten years was a good guarantee as far as the government is concerned. As the agreement states, if in any year Pine Point produces and ships less than 215,000 tons, the mine will have to pay $7.75 for each ton it fails to produce.
According to the experts in my department who are well versed in questions involving

tariffs, the building of railways and the drafting of agreements between the government and railways, this is a fair guarantee in the circumstances. The mine will spend $21 million to build a plant at Pine Point, and Cominco will spend $16 million to enlarge its smelter at Trail. We feel that these two companies are taking a risk. We feel that if they produce at that rate for ten years there is no reason to believe that immediately after that period the traffic will drop off. I think the agreement for ten years is a fair agreement. This is the agreement that is usually concluded in the trade with respect to the period of time and the amount of concentrates.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: In his statement the minister said this was a fair risk, and he has now repeated that comment in another form by saying it is a fair agreement. Is that as far as the minister will go in qualifying the financial soundness of this agreement?

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: As I said earlier, if we take into account the general situation it will be seen to be a very good agreement. I think it is a calculated risk, and that the people of Canada will appreciate that the government has entered into this venture.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
I wish to make one or two
observations based upon the minister's disclosure this morning that in order to cover not merely the maintenance and operating cost but also the amortization of the capital this railway would require to ship approximately 800,000 tons of concentrates a year.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: If there were no other shippers.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: Yes, I will give the condition. I understand that this calculation is based on there being no other traffic. This is a good hard measure-it may not be accurate, of course; it is an estimate, and we recognize that-of the amount of traffic in one form or another that this railway will have to get in order to give a return to the people of Canada. Even though the treasury will not get the capital back directly, presumably it will get it back in indirect benefits through taxation and through reduction of the deficit of the C.N.R., and in that sort of way.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
I am sorry; I do not like my hon. friend to be under the wrong impression. It is the amount that would be derived from the shipment of 800,000 tons of concentrates that would completely amortize the $86 million. It is not the taxation, salaries and things of that sort. It would be strictly the amounts paid by the company-
Canadian National Railways

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
I understand that perfectly. There is no provision in the agreement indicating that it would ever come back to the treasury directly if 800,000 tons were shipped. The only way it could get back to the treasury is through the profits of the C.N.R. or incidentally in an even more indirect way through increased business producing increased revenues, which is a proper consideration. I do not object to it at all. I think we would never develop this country if on every expenditure we said we have to get the return directly. I have never argued that, and no one on this side has ever argued that, but we feel we must be shown there is either a direct or an indirect return. Therefore we really need a very hard assurance that in a reasonable period of time there is going to be traffic of this volume on this railway, or it is not going to make a return. In other words, we have a measuring stick now to measure this proposition in hard terms, namely 800,000 tons of concentrates or its equivalent in other forms of traffic.
Last night the hon. member for Peace River in a rather persuasive intervention-and one understands the incentives to persuasion in the case of the hon. member-sought to show what other traffic there would be on this railway in addition to the concentrates.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: At what page of Hansard?

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: At page 8890. He quoted from the report of the mining commission. I have had a chance this morning to look at the case made by the hon. member for Peace River. He quoted from Mr. Anderson-Thomson, whose qualifications he described very flatteringly. I have never met him and I have no reason to believe he is wrong. In fact in most matters not connected with his riding I would accept the words of the hon. member for Peace River without much question, and I would accept his word about any facts at any time; but when it comes to accepting his opinions, that is another matter.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: I bet it is mutual.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
Well, I hope it is mutual. I would not expect the hon. member to accept my opinion, but I would expect him to accept my word on a matter of fact, and I am sure he would.
The hon. gentleman quoted testimony to the effect that from the potential agricultural traffic both the C.N.R. and C.P.R. can expect an addition to their gross revenues of $2 million per annum; not immediately, of course, but over a period of years that would be a reasonable period of calculating by a businessman. I take it that is what the hon.

Canadian National Railways member meant. I am seeking to make this case in the best possible way, because I want to be lair.
The hon. member then referred to lumber. He said there would be a total yearly revenue-this is not a quotation, and I hope the hon. member will listen very carefully because I want to be sure I am correctly stating the implication of what he said. Perhaps I had better read what he did say:
He indicates that if the total potential of the annual allowable cut is developed, and I do not anticipate that this will happen at once, of course, there will be a total yearly revenue to the two railway companies of $3,600,000.
I do not know whether the hon. gentleman meant gross revenue to both railways, but I assume that since the only other figure was gross revenue to both railways, these are gross revenues. They are not profits; indeed, it is a nice question whether they would ever enter into the realm of profits at all. I feel that approximately $5.5 million of gross revenues from the only other two immediate sources in prospect-and that is not right away, and it is not just to this line mind you, but to the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific all over the country-does not go very far to fill the gap between the
215,000	tons of concentrates and 800,000 tons of concentrates which the minister has indicated his officials consider are really necessary to make this a self-supporting undertaking.
This really points up what we were trying to get, that is precise and hard information that is wanted by my hon. friend from Laurier and me and others who joined with us. This is the point we were trying to make last night, that we should have more than a gleam in the ministers' eye. We should see a probability, not this year, not next year, but a probability, not a possibility, of traffic of this magnitude in order to justify this operation.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
I calculated last night that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate would in all probability make an estimate of the statements I had made. I will not say I did it deliberately, but I left out two other prospects for traffic which I now bring to the attention of the committee. If the hon. member will read page 86 of the report of the commission to which I referred him last night he will find that in addition to the lumber there is a potential of traffic generated by pulp which would be available from this area. I think the hon. gentleman can see that in due course this potential would justify six pulp mills producing 200 tons a day, which would bring about a yearly traffic of $12 million.
I think the hon. member will see on the same page that in addition, once you get to the stage where you have this amount of


business generated you are bound to find that more people will be in the area. There will then be incoming traffic of manufactured and processed goods, the long haul type of carriage, from the central and eastern parts of the continent. As I understand the formula which has been worked out, the profit pattern of railway transportation indicates that manufactured and processed goods of that nature always yield the highest revenue. Therefore when you ship out $5 million to $10 million worth of goods from this area you are bound to have a situation where substantial traffic in processed goods, probably equivalent to the same amount of money, will be shipped in yielding that much revenue to the railways.
This, I think, answers the point raised by the hon. member for Laurier, that this is not the kind of railway where you have to wait until the last tie is laid and the last spike driven before there will be revenue. Once this line has been laid and completed for a distance of 75 miles-and I refer to 75 miles from the south, because I am assuming that is where construction will start-substantial traffic will immediately be generated. I think the cost will be very much less than the average of $170,000 a mile. There will then be railway traffic available on the first 75 miles, and the cost of the construction of that mileage will probably be less than $10 million. In the ensuing years there will be more construction and more traffic generated, both incoming and outgoing. All these are things which hon. members have not taken into account in their calculations.
I should like to refer hon. members to the report of the Gordon commission and the Paley report which, it will be recalled, was a report delivered some years ago to the president of the United States. This report was based on careful calculations of the indicated material requirements of the North American continent. The Paley report coincides pretty well with the Gordon report. They say it is inevitable that over the course of the next 15 to 25 years there will be required of Canada substantial quantities of these lead and zinc concentrates. Mr. Fitzpatrick, the president of Cominco, in a speech he made early this spring in Edmonton, said that in his opinion the opening up of Pine Point would probably lead to the development of the mine and the shipment of concentrates for a greater period than 25 years. This is the statement of a responsible man and indicates the premise on which his company is prepared to expend almost $40 million. Surely, Mr. Chairman, if there are indications of substantial traffic for a greater

period than 25 years, this should be an answer to the very pertinent questions which have been asked.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
Last evening and earlier today we heard statements from the Minister of Transport in an attempt to justify the spending of $66 million of the taxpayers' money for the construction of a railway which could lead to the development of mineral deposits in the far north. I am sure the minister is aware of the fact that in 1956 the Canadian National built 16 miles of railway in northern New Brunswick under similar, but probably much more favourable circumstances. This railway has been used rarely, I think only for the official opening ceremonies.
We have in New Brunswick, in populated and inhabited areas, from 12 to 20 miles from deep-sea ports, over 10 million tons of mineral deposits which are awaiting development. A small portion of this amount could be spent to much better advantage to the taxpayers of this country if the government would, by means of tax incentives or other provisions, stimulate the development of the deposits that are located in these populated areas. Here we are considering the construction of a railway from 500 to 600 miles long which goes almost nowhere, leading to mineral deposits, and those concentrates will have to be transported about 1,000 miles or more before they can be processed.
I repeat that we have right in northeastern New Brunswick 100 million tons of mineral deposits which are idle now, awaiting more advantageous market facilities. I suggest to the minister, therefore, that serious consideration should be given to the provision of facilities for existing mines in areas to which access is easier.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
There are two questions that I do not think have been cleared up to my satisfaction. One of them has to do with the traffic from the various points. I think it is quite clear that from Great Slave lake to Grimshaw, a distance of 438 miles, that is traffic which would belong to the new line; from Grimshaw to Edmonton over the N.A.R., 325 miles, the traffic is divided equally between the two railways; from Edmonton to Calgary, 233 miles, the traffic moves over Canadian National; from Calgary to Tadanac, 460 miles, the traffic moves over the Canadian Pacific. I do not believe it has ever been stated how the traffic will move from the various points to British Columbia ports. There are several lines, as the minister knows. There is the national transcontinental, there
Canadian National Railways is the P.G.E. and there is the Canadian Pacific. What is the division of traffic in so far as the various British Columbia ports are concerned?

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: My information is that it will be 50-50 between the two railways.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: The other question that came to my mind was this. Have the provincial interests been approached at all in connection with the cost of this railway? By that I mean that sometimes when arrangements are not satisfactory to Canadian National Railways, in the financial sense, in connection with a railway of this nature, namely of a developmental character, the provincial authorities are approached to ascertain whether or not they would be willing, because of the natural resource development which will ensue in their province, to contribute a subsidy toward the construction of the line. Were the provincial interests involved here approached in that respect?

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: Not to my knowledge, Mr. Chairman.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
I should like to refer to the first question raised by the hon. member for Laurier, the division of traffic to British Columbia ports. I was not a member of the committee, so I was not able to ask this question during the committee proceedings. I presume the reference here is to concentrates which would be shipped not to Trail or Tadanac but to British Columbia ports for export, presumably from Edmonton. I presume there would be no choice of route up to Grimshaw, and there would be no choice beyond Grimshaw unless a line were built to the P.G.E. Presumably the agreement says the concentrates will be shipped from Edmonton; I read the agreement once and I think it said something about a fair distribution or something of that sort. I must say that my opinion of what a fair distribution would be, having regard to the fact that the taxpayers are putting up all the money to build the railway, would be 100 per cent to the Canadian National Railways. If the taxpayers are going to put up this money, and if the only way we can get back a return on our capital is directly through a Canadian National surplus, I do not see why any traffic should go via the Canadian Pacific where there is a Canadian National line.
There is no Canadian National line between Calgary and Trail, so that traffic has to go by the Canadian Pacific. However, a firm undertaking seems to have been given that the Canadian National will get the traffic between Edmonton and Calgary. During the sessions of the committee on railways

Canadian National Railways air lines and shipping I asked Mr. Gordon a question about this traffic, and I am hoping that my intervention may have had some influence in making sure this traffic did go by Canadian National.
I have nothing against the Canadian Pacific; far from it. However, I see no good reason, if the taxpayers are going to put up the capital to generate this traffic, why the Canadian National should not get all the traffic everywhere it has a line. It seems to me this is one respect in which the government should insist upon this agreement being renegotiated in the interest of the taxpayers.

It will not bring population to the Northwest Territories to the same extent that the western railroads brought it to the prairies, but it may well bring in the years ahead of comparable increase in the wealth of Canada. This railway is quite different from most of the branch lines constructed in recent years which were destined to serve one mine, or a group of mines; its purpose is to open up a whole new region. The fact that there happens to be a potential mine of great value at its northern terminus is a piece of great good fortune, for it will enable this railroad to be built without the long wait for reasonable returns which so often has been the lot of a pioneer railroad.
I quite realize that the Pine Point mine will not pay the whole capital cost of the railway or for the operation of this railway. On the other hand, the Pine Point mine will make a very large contribution to the cost of operation and maintenance of this railway and will contribute, as well, to the capital cost of this line. I sincerely believe, therefore, that, using the arguments that have been put forward by Mr. Robertson, this is a railroad that is completely different from the other railroads that have been built in the past, or from the branch lines we are building, like the Mattagami line. I am sure it must come as a shock to every other member of this house. Of course we can realize the handicap that this party is operating under, since it has no members from western Canada to represent it in the house or to advise it. When one considers the attitude that they have adopted in this debate there is little wonder that they have no members from that part of the country.
They have professed to put forward to the people of this country that the only thing they can see in the whole northwest of this country is one mine, and they say if we build a railroad up there that is the only thing we are going to have. Well, surely, Mr. Speaker, nobody in this country has as little faith as that. I cannot understand how a political party, professing to be a major party in this country and representing all parts of it, could possibly or conceivably take such an attitude toward the development of northwestern Canada. As I pointed out the other

day, this is not the first time they have adopted that attitude. When it came time to build the Canadian Pacific Railway to unite Canada into a nation and open up the western part of the country they adopted a similar attitude; they have adopted the same attitude toward this railroad. Some 30 years ago Mackenzie King promised to build it but they have found one excuse after another to put it off. Now we have the same suggestion from the hon. member for Laurier again; put it off again for another six months; it will not hurt. I suppose in his view, after his party put it off for 30 years, another six months will not hurt. I can only say that I think the people in this country are fortunate in having a government in office today that is not going to approach the problems facing Canada with an attitude such as that.
Here we have an opportunity to develop the whole northern part of this country in a way that has been outlined by the government of the province of British Columbia in support of this measure, and by the commissioner of the Northwest Territories, and by the many briefs that were put before the royal commission which investigated the route. We are in a position where we can build this railroad and be guaranteed its operating and maintenance costs for a period of ten years. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) professes to tell us that he does not believe it is possible under these conditions for this railway to operate at a profit. No returns are we going to get, he says. There is apparently no return to the taxpayers from this. Well, I dare say even if what he said were true, even if we were spending $86 million and the Canadian taxpayer was not going to get something back in dollars and cents, the benefit obtained by developing that part of the country would be worth the money.
It has been pointed out already that there are many financial benefits which will be gained from it. I refer in that connection to what was said by the commissioner of the Northwest Territories when he pointed out the amount of ore that was going to be shipped fom this one mine. When the possibility of building the line was investigated in those days the estimate was considerably lower than what was signed for in this agreement which provides for 215,000 tons each year. At that time they were planning on shipping 147,000 tons and the commissioner pointed out that the federal treasury would benefit to the extent of $3.5 million a year just from that one thing alone. We are now guaranteed in this agreement that we are going to have that shipment for ten years so there will be a return to the taxpayer in taxes from the
Canadian National Railways operation of this one mine of an amount of $40 million to $50 million. The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate tell us that there is going to be no return to the taxpayer. In addition to that, as I have pointed out, the railroad is guaranteed its operating and maintenance costs for a period of ten years. Surely, with that potential development of northwest Canada in mind it seems incredible to believe that any member in this house would rise in his place and under those conditions say that this railroad cannot operate at a profit.
I do not want to take up any more of the time of the house on this matter. The various views have been put forward. That is shown by the fact that the biggest argument in favour of this railway, and the one the minister falls back on every time he is pressed, is the evidence given by Mr. Robertson before the Gordon commission. When was that evidence given? It was given under the previous administration. Anybody familiar with the real history of these things is aware that not only were there many blueprints but that many of the projects had been started.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
Well, the new Aklavik was started by the previous government. Most of


the roads were started by them. The new school program was started. I must say that the present government is to be commended for carrying on these programs. I have never complained about that. But the way in which they denature history in the way they have consistently done is another example of the fact that between June, 1891 and June, 1957, in the Prime Minister's book nothing happened in this country.
In the days when Mr. St. Laurent was Prime Minister it was not only the north which was being developed. There never was at any period in the history of this country so much capital development, both public and private, as there was in the years from 1947 to 1957, and the statistics which have been repeatedly brought before this house by the present government-reluctantly, I admit- go to show it. The evidence which was given in the other place before their committee on manpower and a great deal of other statistical evidence indicates very clearly that this progress stopped in the year 1958. It simply stopped.
Now the Prime Minister talks about the north as though Alberta were the only part of the north. It is not, you know. There is also a north which was developed right after the war by private enterprise in Labrador. Here was a company which paid for its own railway; it did not get it paid for by the taxpayer. I say we have to look at a question of this kind in broad prospective. We have to ask ourselves: if we are going to spend this amount of money out of the treasury without getting it back, without any service charge, is this the best place to do it? I say that the government has not yet made that case.
I do not know whether I should refer to this or not, and I do not know how my reference to it will be received by the house. However, I think most of us think the late Mr. C. D. Howe did have something to do with the development of this country and that he did have a good capacity to appraise a proposition and decide whether it was a good thing or not. I remember speaking to him a year or two ago-perhaps it was two or three years ago; it was since I have been in opposition-precisely on the subject of this Pine Point railway. The observation he made to me at that time was this: This railway, or some other means of transport if technology moves fast enough, must be provided, because that mine is a very good mine and there is no doubt it will be exploited sooner or later. Perhaps it will not be too long before it is exploited. But it is a very valuable property, and when it becomes really exploitable, the people who own it will

not hesitate to exploit it. That, after all, is something we have to take into account.
This mine will not be lost if this railway is not built immediately. I noticed the other day that Dr. Solandt, one of the vice presidents of the C.N.R., said that what the railways most needed was research-basic research, not merely research into accounting and that sort of thing. It may very well be we shall see technological developments which will make it possible to provide transport very much cheaper than the present arrangements contemplate. This would be in the interests of everyone. It seems to me no one can say that because we are insisting that this should be a good project and a good bargain for the Canadian people before it is allowed to proceed, that this means we are against national development. When I say no one can say it, I know it will be said. It is probably being said already. But I suggest, without regard to what will be said about these things, that when the facts are such as they are in this case we must assure ourselves that this is the best use which can be made of these funds in the interests of all the Canadian people in the year 1962-I mention that year because this money certainly cannot be spent in 1961-and from then on. It is true that there is in contemplation the construction of 400 miles of line through a very rich part of the country which undoubtedly has a great future. But even the Minister of Finance is slowly beginning to discover that the resources which can be extracted from the taxpayers of Canada are limited. For this reason I have no hesitation whatever in standing up and being counted in opposition, not to the principle of the railway-after all, who would be opposed to it-but to this particular way of doing things.
I remember when I was a small boy living in the bush in northern Manitoba. We had on the wall of our dining room a map of Manitoba. The Hudson's Bay Railway was indicated by a dotted line and there was another dotted line running north from the Gypsumville line to connect with the Hudson's Bay Railway. I remember thinking that some day that railway would be built and the main route to Europe would be through Winnipeg right past our door to the Hudson's Bay Railway. That railway has not been built yet. We are all a little sentimental about these things and I confess that if there is $66 million in the treasury to spend on a railway I would rather see that railway built than one in Northern Alberta. That is just a personal preference, but I would not expect these things to be decided on the basis of personal preference. I would expect us to weigh the merits of the two and then decide
Canadian National Railways which would be best in the national interest. And let no one say that a railway through northern Manitoba such as I have described would not open up a lot of valuable territory. It would reduce very considerably the distance over which the International Nickel Company would have to ship their concentrates. There is a lot of pulpwood in that country, a great new electrical development going on at the Grand Rapids. However, we are not asking the taxpayers to build that railway in northern Manitoba. We are asking them to build one in northern Alberta. Either would contribute to northern development. So would a railway to Hamilton Falls in Labrador, and to Goose Bay. There is no question but that there are tremendous potential resources in Labrador. But would the taxpayers of Canada, without some reasonable assurance that within a reasonable time those potentialities were going to become actual, be justified in doing that? I think we have to apply the same yardstick to all these proposals. Let us, of course, believe in our country, but do not let us do things which will turn out to be bad bargains and discourage people in the future from believing in this country, which certainly is not going to be destroyed if we take a second look at this proposition and come back here next year with a better one.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to participate in this debate but I cannot leave unchallenged some of the statements made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill). The hon. gentleman has said that we should be very careful about proceeding with the bill because ill founded schemes could very well set back northern development. I live in the north, Mr. Speaker, and I have travelled across the Canadian north. In my view nothing has so set back northern development as did the 22 years of Liberal rule when a complete void and vacuum existed with respect to the development of the north. The hon. gentleman spoke of ill founded schemes. We could point to schemes that have been inordinately costly and that are a continuing drain on the taxpayers who live in the north. One project immediately comes to mind, the Whitehorse sewer and water system constructed during the Liberal administration at a cost of millions of dollars for a city of 20,000 people at a stage of development when there were only 2,500 people there. Is this the kind of scheme the hon. gentleman speaks of when he refers to ill founded schemes?
The hon. gentleman said the construction of the railway at this time might set back the undertaking of important projects that should be undertaken in the north. The party of

Canadian National Railways which the hon. gentleman is a member should have thought oi many projects that should have been undertaken in the north while they were in power, but they did not. I wonder, as must a great many hon. members of this house, whether these great plans for northern Canada, of which the Liberals now speak, were kept for 22 years in the same cupboard as their great shelf of public works which was supposed to be there when we took office in 1957? The cupboard was bare, these great plans are empty dreams and the words of hon. gentlemen opposite echo hollowly when they seek to claim credit for undertaking projects in the north.
The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Che-vrier) said he had been in the north several times. I have never seen the hon. gentleman in the north. Since I have lived there I have seen only one Liberal minister of northern affairs and national resources in the north, Mr. Lesage, who visited in 1953. I have never seen the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate in the north.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext: You were fortunate.

subtopic: CONSTRUCTION OF LINE TO GREAT SLAVE LAKE
speechtext:
Perhaps this is the explanation for the apparent and appalling ignorance of the hon. gentleman when he begins describing things that are happening in the north about which he has no knowledge. He does not know about them because he has not been there. I know that in the last three years more projects have been brought to completion in the north than were brought to completion in the previous decade, the reason being that this government implemented them, took action.
I also know of many projects that were turned down by the previous administration. One example is the road to the oil fields in Eagle Plains. The former government was asked by private industry to assist in the building of a trail to this area to the extent of contributing $300,000, but hon. gentlemen said they would not give a single nickel to assist in the development of this potentially rich area. They would not admit the possibility that reserves might be there. The same attitude is apparent with regard to this railway. This is yet another example of the waffling in which hon. members of the opposition have been engaging during even the short time I have been sitting here. Their leader has condemned the national development program of this government, and the policy designed to bring about northern development. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and I had an exchange a few months ago during which I tried to have the hon. member retract his "igloo to igloo" statement, the position he took with respect to communications in the northern part of

this country. He would not do so on that occasion nor has he done so since. The reason is apparent. Hon. gentlemen opposite simply do not believe in the riches the north country has to contribute to the over-all development of Canada.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have lauded Mr. St. Laurent as the great northern developer. Not one single project of any size or importance was undertaken in the Yukon territory by the government of Mr. St. Laurent. We asked for roads and projects of all kinds but all were cast aside and rejected. Why? The hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate speaks about projects for vote catching. I suspect the reason that the Liberals rejected the northern projects for the development of the nation as a whole is that there were more votes to be caught in some of the other provinces that are more heavily populated. The remarks of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate are absolutely false and I give the lie to them. I do not ascribe to the hon. gentleman any motive in his saying these things. I believe he says them out of ignorance. The hon. gentleman has never been in the north and does not know what is going on.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the willingness of the house to expedite consideration of this measure on second reading in the manner just now indicated, and in the same spirit I can assure the house that I propose to be very brief.
This measure, Bill No. C-122, was introduced in the house on July 12. That introduction followed a discussion in the committee of the whole on the resolution stage. In introducing the resolution in the committee I set forth at I think some length, Mr. Speaker, the features of the proposed measure and the reasons why the government is asking the house to adopt this measure as one which will contribute and we believe contribute substantially, to an improvement in dominion-provincial fiscal relations.
I think it would be quite superfluous to repeat the reasons which I advanced in the statement at that time. The remarks were recorded in Hansard at pages 7910 to 7930. I do not, of course, claim to have occupied 20 pages of Hansard with my remarks, but those pages included the quite extensive tables which were placed on record with the consent of the house and which contain quite an encyclopaedia of tabular material in relation to this subject which it was thought would be of assistance to the house in the approach to the consideration of the bill on second reading. I think, therefore, I have nothing to add to the remarks that I made on July 11.
I think I should say to the house that when we reach the committee stage I will be introducing an amendment, and perhaps I should say just a word about the nature of that amendment at this point. In order that the crown in right of the dominion may make deductions at the source on account of provincial tax from payments to its own employees or in respect of other payments made out of the consolidated revenue fund or by an agent of Her Majesty in right of Canada, statutory authority for this purpose is required. It is proposed that the bill be amended to provide such statutory authority. Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, when we reach the committee stage of the bill I shall be introducing an amendment to clause 6 of the bill which will add to that clause a subclause 3.
