maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words must be an expression of profound disappointment at the brevity of the speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). That regret is not because I am fond of hearing the Minister of Finance but because I hoped to have a rest until half past seven before I was obliged to take up the time of the house again. But the Minister of Finance has told us that except for the amendment, of which he has given us notice, he had his say on July 11 at the resolution stage and he has nothing in particular to add.
I had hoped and had rather expected that the minister would at least deal with those developments which have taken place since his speech on July 11. I refer to the protests that have come from at least half the premiers of the provinces of this country about the inadequacy of the bill from their point of view and about the arrogant manner in which the government has treated the provincial governments and their representations.
Knowing how thorough the Minister of Finance is when he replies to arguments, I had expected that he would attempt to deal with these protests. However, apparently the decision of the government is that the views of the provincial governments as expressed by the heads of those governments are to be ignored. I do not think that some of them can be ignored by those of us on this side of the house and in the course of my remarks I shall have some observations to make about them.
First of all I wish to say something about the measure itself. The purpose of this measure, as I see it, is to do two things. It is first of all to provide for a redistribution to the provinces of certain sums of money that are collected from the national taxpayers and paid into the national treasury, a redistribution of these sums to the provinces to be used in any way the provincial legislatures may see fit for provincial purposes. The other purpose of the legislation is to empower the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) to collect for the provinces which wish to have their taxes collected for them, their income taxes both personal and corporate. It seems to me that this more or less exhausts the fundamental purposes of the bill, though the measure contains a good many ancillary features which can be dealt with at the committee stage.
I think it would not be amiss to say a word or two about why there should be any taxes


at all collected by virtue of action of this parliament to be used for provincial purposes. When the Minister of Finance was on this side of the house he used to repeat arguments which have been made in other times and by distinguished Liberals about how desirable it would be at all times to have the taxes imposed and collected by those who spent the money. As Sir Wilfrid Laurier said in 1907 when he was proposing to increase the subsidies to the provinces, that is unexceptionable as a general abstract proposition. I do not think there is anyone who would argue that apart from attendant circumstances there is anything to be said in favour of one body collecting taxes for another body to spend. If we had ideal theoretical conditions that would probably be the way in which it could be done. But, as Sir Wilfrid Laurier also pointed out in 1907, there would have been one little difficulty. If we had adhered to this fundamental general principle there would never have been Canadian confederation and there would be no Canadian nation today. I say this because for all the provinces except Ontario-for all the original four except Ontario-and for every other province which has come into the Canadian union since, the subsidy has been a sine qua non. Without it the province could not have afforded to become part of the union. That has always been true, and for more than half a century after confederation the greater part of provincial revenues was derived from the federal treasury. I shall not deal further with that matter because I believe one of my colleagues will have more to say about it. There seems to be in certain parts of the country a profound ignorance of these plain historical facts, though these facts are easily ascertainable by anyone who wants to look them up.
Notwithstanding the fact that the foundation of confederation was subsidies, it happened in the thirties that there was a great recession in this country and for the first time we had to face the necessity either of letting people starve or of supporting them out of public funds on a great scale. The burden of doing this was far too great for any of the provinces to undertake on the basis of the taxation capacity the provinces had in those days. It was, of course, bankrupting to most of the provinces. One of the provinces which now boasts of being more financially orthodox than any other defaulted on the interest payments on its bonds. Other provinces were only saved from bankruptcy by hand-outs from the provincial treasury and, in the case of Manitoba, where I lived at that time, by the imposition of taxation of a severity which no province has ever experienced since. The problem was so great that by 1935 it had to

be dealt with in one or two ways. This was recognized before the election of 1935. The present lieutenant governor of Quebec was, in fact, chairman of a committee of this house which considered this problem of federal-provincial relations in that year. This may seem odd to the ears of some people in the province in which he is now the representative of the crown, but that committee recommended centralization as a cure for this problem. That, of course, has been the historical position of the Tory party, and Mr. Gagnon and Mr. Bennett, in whose government he later served, were, of course, merely following that tradition. But after the election of 1935 a different position was taken by the new government and a great royal commission, perhaps the greatest royal commission ever appointed in this country, was established by Mr. Mackenzie King and Mr. Ernest Lapointe in 1937, the commission which is generally known as the Rowell-Sirois commission on dominion-provincial relations. That commission was instructed to approach this problem from the opposite point of view, not from the point of view of taking services away from the provinces and centralizing them in Ottawa, but from the point of view of finding the means to place all the provinces in a position to perform the services which the founders of confederation intended them to have. That, of course, was the historic Liberal approach to the problem and it has been the Liberal approach ever since. Unfortunately this problem was not finally solved before the second world war, and in the second world war, of course, many of the problems of the provinces disappeared because we had over full employment. During most of the years of the war every provincial government had substantial surpluses and the problem was temporarily obscured. Indeed, the easiest course at the end of the war would have been to go back to the situation as it was in 1937 or 1939 and start all over again.
That was not done. It was not done for two reasons. It was not done, in the first place, because the provincial governments did not want to do it. The man who took the initiative in bringing this question forward was the then premier of Ontario, Mr. George Drew. Neither did the federal government want a return to the old position. They felt there should be a more constructive approach to the whole problem. In 1945 and 1946 a prolonged effort was made to get an agreement on a very broad base. Unfortunately, it was not possible to get an agreement, and the federal government then made certain proposals to the provinces which all but two of them accepted-propositions which had the effect of putting the provinces in funds in order that they might provide
Dominion-Provincial Relations their own services. In 1952, when those agreements expired, new agreements based on much the same foundation although somewhat changed were made, and on this occasion all the provinces participated with the exception of Quebec. Ontario, with a new premier, came in in the meantime.
It became increasingly apparent that through no fault of the federal government but through a self denying ordinance of the premier of Quebec of that day these arrangements were resulting in large sums of money being collected in nine and later in ten of the provinces and being disbursed for the benefit of people in only eight or nine. This was a situation which no Canadian interested in the unity of his country could contemplate with anything but sorrow, and the position was seriously aggravated when the financial situation of the province of Quebec became such as to cause anxiety. Because it was not willing to participate in the existing system, the government of that province put a tax on its people and this meant they were doubly taxed and getting no benefit from one of the taxes. I am not criticizing that government for that at this stage at all. I am simply stating the facts.
I well remember that at that time Mr. St. Laurent said one day: "I do not think we can go on being unfair because another government is, in our opinion, unreasonable". He and his officials then devoted a great deal of time and energy to devising a stop gap arrangement. That was recognized as a stop gap and a real search was made to find a better system in 1955 and 1956, accounts of which have been placed on Hansard times without number and I do not intend to weary the committee by repeating them now.
In my opinion a very substantial improvement was found. To paraphrase Mr. St. Laurent's words which I do not have here, it was the best thing that had been thought of up to that time. But he did not claim it was perfect. That was the system of equalization.
Now, what is equalization? What is the basis of equalization as it was established at that time? It is very simple. Mr. Harris expressed it very well in one of his budget speeches when he said that what we collect here in Ottawa in the federal treasury is collected from the people of Canada for the benefit of all the people of Canada and that it should benefit all the people of Canada equally and that that is the only basis on which we can safely proceed if we wish to have a united country.
The principle of equalization is very simple. It is that a certain fixed proportion of the revenues from the personal income tax and the corporation income tax, not fixed for all
8944	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Dominion-Provincial Relations time but capable of being varied from time to time, should be allotted to the provincial governments. They should not be forced to impose the tax themselves but a certain proportion should be allotted to them for provincial purposes. In addition, any of those provinces where that allotment was less than the average of the collections of the two wealthiest provinces-that is to say, the provinces with the wealthiest taxpayers, on the average-the deficiency should be made up by an equalization payment so that the provincial governments of all our provinces would have, per head, the same amount to spend on their people out of these great national taxes. In other words, equality.
It was not quite equality, however, because to have complete equality one should have taken the highest province. There were certain objections to doing that which were put forward at the time by some of the provincial governments. It was felt that it should be the two highest provinces. I admit that personally I think it would have been more completely fair to have taken the highest, but it made very little difference because it was averaged not just between the two figures but with the population taken into account, and when that was taken into account the difference was slight whether Ontario was taken alone or whether Ontario and British Columbia were taken together.
That was the principle of equalization that was embodied in the statute of 1956. Indeed it was the basis of that statute but it was not the only basis. The statute of 1956 gave to the provincial governments a greater freedom of choice of physical expedients, plus equalization, plus redistribution from the federal treasury than any other scheme before. But equalization was paid as a matter of right. No province had to come and apply for it. The provinces did not have to sign for it. It was paid as a matter of right. Any province that wished to do so could rent to the federal government any of the three tax fields, the personal income tax, the corporation income tax or the succession duty, and not impose a tax, or it could impose any or all of the taxes, as it saw fit.
There was complete freedom. In addition to that, any province could impose any additional tax it liked although it could not get an abatement of such tax. In other words, no strings of any kind were attached except those which the provincial governments themselves wished to place upon their own freedom of action because they felt it was a better deal for them.
No province suffered through not making a tax rental agreement. The tax rental arrangement was a purely optional matter. The only

thing about that which was completely new and really important was the equalization. Coupled with that, of course, there were certain provisions for stabilization.
I do not know whether or not some of the provincial premiers had a prescience about what might happen after 1956 or 1957 but some of them seemed to wish a floor on what they would get. I am sure that if they had been confident that the Liberal government was going to stay in office they would not have worried about a floor because they would have expected the kind of progress, expansion and growth which there was under the Liberal administration in 1956; but perhaps foreseeing what would happen in 1957 and fearing the financial mismanagement of the country after that date, they insisted on having a floor which was called stabilization, and this was provided. I shall not go into the details of it because this subject is not before us at the moment. As a result of what happened under the present government some of the provinces had to rely upon that stabilization to some degree and apparently are going to increasingly rely upon it.
We were told in 1957 during the course of a celebrated election campaign that all this was going to be changed, that a new era was going to dawn in federal-provincial relations, that if the Conservatives won the election there would be a state of harmony between the federal government and the provinces which had not existed before, that very much greater latitude would be given to them, that their revenues would be substantially increased and that the revenues of the federal treasury would be correspondingly reduced. Of course, this was all going to be done out of these great surpluses that the Liberals had so wickedly been building up over the years. It is perhaps not surprising that these great expectations were not fulfilled. Perhaps one cannot accurately describe them any longer as expectations; they are simply historic relics today.
Some of us recall these events and perhaps it is worth while reminding hon. members of the committee of some of them. At Massey Hall in Toronto on April 27, 1957 the present premier of Ontario was on his feet to address the opening Conservative rally of the election campaign of that year. What did Mr. Frost say? He said:
We have been compelled to impose unfair taxation on our people because of the failure of the federal government to face up to our problems-
Not "its problems" but "our problems". I continue:
-these are going to increase unless a just solution is found and the man who is going to find that solution is this man who is sitting on the platform.

Well, "this man" is now the Prime Minister of Canada. The solution to Mr. Frost's problem, as everyone in this chamber knows and is reminded of every time he makes a purchase in any shop in this province today was not found, except indirectly, by this man. Indeed, of all those who were disillusioned and disappointed by the outcome of the promises of that fair spring of 1957 there could be no more disillusioned man than the retiring premier of Ontario.

The plain fact is, of course, that we were told that right after the election in 1957 there would be a federal-provincial conference. It would be the first thing that would happen. Well, it happened in November 1957 and, lo and behold, instead of a solution there were a few platitudinous observations made by the Prime Minister at the beginning of that conference and then the premiers stated, as they had been encouraged to by the election speeches, what they thought they ought to get out of the treasury, and then they got a cold towel in their faces from the Minister of Finance who had been adding with that capacity to add which we know is unrivalled in this country. He had found out how much this was going to cost and he told the premiers what he felt it was going to cost and suggested that they go home. He promised that they would be back in January.

If the minister does not think his speech was a suggestion to them to go home he has a very poor capacity, as I think he has, to calculate the effect of
90205-6-564
Dominion-Provincial Relations his own performances. At any rate, they came to pray and they went home to mourn. But they were told they were going to have another chance. This great harmony, this agreement, this understanding that was going to be reached, this new era of brotherly love and harmony between provincial premiers and the government of Canada that was to be ushered in in 1957 was going to come in 1958 at the next conference.
We know what the next conference was like. The next conference was held by way of the telegraph companies, and some of the premiers were not even present on time; they read about it first in the newspapers. The minister told them they were going to get a small slice on account of the great expectations and they were going to get it right away. They were not going to be consulted about it; it was going to be put through parliament quickly, and in the words of the minister, not on that occasion but on previous occasions, they could take it or leave it.
Well, of course, it was money; it was some more money and they took it. It was also before the 1958 election, and that is all they have ever seen. Then we had the great period of the minister's study groups, and that went on for a long time. Finally it was apparent that this whole business could not be stalled off much longer, and in 1960 the provincial premiers were again called back to Ottawa for another round. Before they came here the minister was asked whether this was with a view to improving the existing arrangements which had been so dreadful, of course, before 1957, but which were carried on all during this period, and the minister said, "Oh, no, all these agreements are in operation; this is for the next period after March 31, 1962." The premiers came here and I am sure they expected to be told what ideas were in the minds of the federal government. Well, they did not get any ideas; they did not get any suggestions in detail but they did get an assurance-and I want to read it and put it on Hansard because I think this is one of the most solemn assurances ever given to the provincial governments by any Prime Minister in the history of this country. This assurance will be found on page 10 of the report of the proceedings of the dominion-provincial conference, 1960. It is part of the opening speech delivered by the Prime Minister as chairman of that conference, and the pledge reads:
I want to make this abundantly clear on behalf of the dominion government that whatever the ultimate decision may be the principle of equalization must be preserved.
Equalization, the second component, is a payment by Canada to the provinces to bring the per capita return from the three taxes at standard rates up to the average per capita yield in the two provinces in which per capita yield is highest.
8946	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Relations For provinces in which the tax potential is relatively low, this principle is the most important.
It might be noted in passing that earlier arrangements did not recognize the principle of equalization explicity although it was to some extent implicit in the "per capita" basis of payment.
An then, these words:
Again I wish to emphasize that the federal government remains firmly committed to the principle of equalization and of financial assistance to those provinces in which incomes and taxable capacity are below those of the richer provinces.
What has happened to that pledge I will deal with in the second instalment of these remarks.

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Fleming (Eglinton) for the

maintopic: AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Before we adjourned at dinner time, I had just read the undertaking that had been given by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on July 25 and which appears in the proceedings of the dominion-provincial conference for the year 1960. I had expressed the strongest possible approval of that pledge. I did so at the resolution stage and I want again to make it very clear that I do not know of any better definition of equalization than the definition that was given by the Prime Minister. Had he stuck to the position he had taken on July 25, 1960 in this solemn undertaking to the provinces, I do not believe we would have had a very long debate tonight. While all the provincial governments would no doubt be anxious to get a larger share of the tax money, they all would recognize as was recognized certainly by the opposition in this house, that the basis of this equalization was just and fair. This basis was accepted by the government for four years.
Now, I do not want to leave out another aspect of this matter. It is true that in 1958, for the fiscal year 1958-59 and subsequent fiscal years up to the present one, the present government did increase the amount of the equalization. They did not change the basis in any respect whatever from the basis that was established on the recommendation of Mr. St. Laurent and Mr. Harris in 1956. However, they did increase the amount and that increase was undoubtedly a very welcome increase to the provincial governments. It was a good deal less than they would have liked to get. I might say parenthetically right here, and I am looking at a former provincial premier as I say this, that as long as we live in this vale of tears where men are imperfect, we will never have provincial governments completely satisfied with the share of the total revenues that is available to them. If they were satisfied I am afraid that many national services would be starved. This is something that anyone with any experience in these matters has to recognize.
It was recognized in 1956 by all of the premiers, even Mr. Duplessis who on all previous occasions had taken a completely intransigent attitude that this was such a marked improvement and that he would take the money, and he did take it. It was a very good thing for him that he did because he would not have been able to carry on much

longer without it. It was a very good thing for the people of Quebec, too, that he did. The fact of the matter was that every premier at that conference recognized that the new basis of equalization was a great improvement over the old tax rental system. I think it is fair to say that there was no premier who would have been caught dead admitting that he had got quite enough. It might be that in retrospect they did not get quite enough. I would not be prepared to argue that point very strenuously. It may be that in the circumstances it might have been better to make the dividend a little larger than it was.
However, I am talking about the principle, and as I say this principle has been continued up to the present. There was an improvement made in the amount, quite a substantial improvement in 1958 by the present government. The present government did something else in 1958 for which I have never ceased to give them credit. I spoke for our party on this matter when the measure was first before the house and I expressed our approval of it. I commended the government for it and I have commended the government for it ever since. It is really about the only thing I can commend this government upon wholeheartedly, and its unique character makes me all the more willing to do so. I refer to the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants. I say theoretically and I also say in a practical sense that I believe it would have been better if suggestions such as those which were made by Mr. Henry Hicks and by the then premier of New Brunswick (Mr. Flemming) who is now here, to establish these payments on a basis of principle had been accepted. I think those suggestions would be better than the fixed amount. I also think that it should apply in theory-I hope it would never apply in practice-to any province that found itself in similar circumstances. I think that would give it a wider and solider foundation. I am not seeking to embarrass him but I doubt that the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Flemming) would disagree much with that statement. I know there are many people in the Atlantic provinces who agree with me. But notwithstanding that fact, substantially the same end was achieved by what was done.
At that time it was stressed by the government that equalization alone was not enough to meet the special needs of the Atlantic provinces and that something in addition to equalization was needed, and I stress this point. The two things were kept quite distinct. The minister emphasized that fact very strongly when he put the matter before the house, namely that they were quite separate and distinct things, and that this was something new done by the new government. It 90205-6-564i
Dominion-Provincial Relations was something new and it was something which was very creditable. I doubt perhaps whether they would have done it with the same alacrity if they had had then the majority which they had after March 31, 1958. However, that is entering the field of speculation and perhaps I should not do so. I should underline the fact that they have done nothing more for the provinces since then. Once they obtained a majority they just stonewalled the provinces up until the time they finally called the conference for the next round in 1960 and they put nothing before them in July except a few pious platitudes.
Then came the debacle in October. What happened in October was this. I suppose it must have been one of those days after the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) had had a bad night, when he had been thinking about his successive deficits and the terrible situation into which he had got the finances of this country. But at any rate the government decided to go right back to 1867. They said, "No more of this progress, no more of this improvement with the growth of the country, no more of this improvement with the growth of population." They said, "You will get $220 million this year and this is all you will get from now on." They said, "Of course we are not saying this is final. This is just a suggestion. We hope you will take it kindly. You can get together and divide it up in any way you like." This is the way in which you get harmony. You toss a bone to a number of- perhaps I should not describe the premiers in that way. Perhaps I had better pause, Mr. Speaker, in that analogy and let each hon. member go on for himself. As a device for the promotion of harmony, to say to 10 provincial premiers "You can have this much money; now you go off by yourselves and divide it up", I cannot think of any better way to get discord than that. It really is infallible. It is sure. It is bound to work and it did work, but not exactly in the way in which the government expected it to work. They did not get harmony but they got unanimity. As the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) pointed out at the resolution stage, the premiers were just falling over one another in condemning the government for the treatment they received at that conference. We all remember the Toronto Star and the anthology they had. The Minister of Finance remembers it well. He rises and denounces it every time it is mentioned. But there they were in black and white, what each of them said about it. I do not need to put it on the record again. It is in Hansard of last July 11 for those who care to read.

As my hon. friend the Acting Leader of the Opposition has said, it was unanimous condemnation. The government was rather nervous about it. Then Mr. Frost was pressed to bring down his budget in January. He rose in his place in the legislature one day in January and said, "I cannot bring down a budget because the government at Ottawa cannot make up its mind what it is going to do and I cannot bring in a budget until I find out what they are going to do." Then we asked the usual questions which it was the duty of an opposition to ask, and we received the usual replies which we receive from this government and which are not very illuminating, that some time in the future in due course if we are good boys, we would be told.
Then there was going to be a supply day the following Monday. Apparently the Minister of Finance or some other member of the government either heard or guessed that the opposition might bring in a vote of want of confidence based on federal-provincial relations. What a scurrying around there must have been over the week end because finally the minister came into the house that day and he could hardly contain himself. Of course, he does not sit in the corner but in every other respect he was like Little Jack Horner. So all of a sudden, out came the plum, namely this letter to the premiers. They had not had time to get it then. He was taking no chances with the post office or the Canadian National Telegraphs. He was getting it out through parliament. This letter told the premiers that there was going to be another conference that Santa Claus was not quite dead after all, because there was going to be what was called a growth factor in the equalization. We were having a debate, Mr. Speaker; and in the olden days in Canada the purpose of debates in this house used to be to illuminate a subject and to inform-

speechtext: As I was saying, we sought to find out what was meant by growth factor. We tried every device that was known to an opposition to get the definition of it. We obtained none. They were faced with a deadline. Then at the last moment, just as the clock was about to strike 12, they had to produce something so they called it a growth factor, but they did not know what kind of growth factor it was going to be. They had not even decided what kind of fertilizer to use at that time.

speechtext:
All they knew was that if they stuck by this principle that they had proposed in October, this $220 million and no more, they would have had the whole country against them, led by the premier of Ontario. So they had to do something about it. When the conference came in February they produced the scheme that they have now produced and which I intend to try to analyse very briefly and in a non-statistical way.
I think we have to start from the premise that the government was very irked by certain effects of the equalization plan. They were very irked by the fact that a very considerable equalization payment was made to the government of Quebec. Somehow or other they do not seem to have the same enthusiasm for the government of Quebec that they had in May and June of 1960. I do not know why, but they do not.
They were also very much irked in more ways than one by the government of British Columbia. They felt that government ought

to be taught a lesson. They were apparently outraged by the fact that the government of Alberta got a substantial equalization payment and they felt something had to be done about that because Alberta was apparently considered too rich to deserve it.
They were also concerned about the fact that somehow or other, without spending much money, they had to scratch around and find a little more for the premier of Ontario; not, of course, what they had promised; not what the advertisements had promised in 1957, but another dividend. He was getting pretty restive after four years and he was not going to be content even with the sales tax unless he got some more out of the federal treasury; not directly, because Ontario got nothing directly, but indirectly from the federal government withdrawing from the field and leaving him to cultivate it at no extra cost to the taxpayer.
So they devised a scheme which they were pleased to call equalization but which is an utter travesty of equalization. They decided, instead of equalizing revenues so that all Canadians wherever they lived were treated alike, to use the national average as the basis. What effect did that have? That had been one of the formulae that had been considered in 1955 and 1956-I know that very well-and rejected because it was so unfair. But the government decided to try to use it. They got results from using it which would have been so unfavourable to the poorer provinces-in fact, to half the provinces-that they simply did not dare to produce that by itself.
Even so it was not doing enough harm to Alberta's position. Therefore they thought they would bring in some notion of taxes on natural resources. They got from the bureau of statistics some mysterious figure, and then they tossed it into the salad, mixed it up a little bit more and got the machine to crank out a figure to see how that worked. That did the trick as far as Alberta and British Columbia were concerned. It cut them down. It of course improved Ontario's position quite materially; and it cut Quebec down, which they were very anxious to do. This would have been fine, but it also cut down Manitoba. They just did not see how they could possibly cut Manitoba down.

maintopic: AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext: They were following John then.

maintopic: AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
After all, Manitoba had a Tory government. So they had to start the mixer working again and see if they could throw something else into the hopper, some other factor of some kind or other, and get something that would come out politically right. Whether is was just, whether it was
Dominion-Provincial Relations fair, whether it was based on any principle did not matter, as long as it would bring the right political effect.
Then they said, "Well, if any province under our new scheme is going to get less than it got under the old scheme, it can stick to the old scheme". That fixed up Manitoba. Well, it did not fix up Manitoba, as I will show in a minute, but at least it did not make Manitoba's position quite as bad as it would otherwise have been. But of course it had the terrible disadvantage that it applied to Quebec also, and to Saskatchewan.
What has happened, sir, as a result of using all these shenanigans instead of following a basis of principle? All these various factors were put in to try to achieve at no cost, or very little cost to the treasury, some predetermined result. Then there was another gimmick for the Atlantic provinces. Of course, under this new equalization formula they were away below what they would have been under the old formula. So the minister said, "Toss them another $10 million under the Atlantic provinces grants and call it equalization. Mix it all up together. Then say, after mixing up the equalization, the Atlantic provinces grants and everything else, that they are not to get any less than they got before". We remember when the minister brought in the Atlantic provinces grants. In the first place he said they were separate from equalization. They were-

maintopic: AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext: Which you approved.

maintopic: AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Which we approved and which I still approve. He said they were something separate and distinct, which was needed, quite apart from equalization. But now they are in the mix, in the salad, as the machine turns around.
This had a wonderful effect because it really produced a result that was better for Prince Edward Island, and for Nova Scotia for the time being it was quite a considerable improvement. For Newfoundland there was some improvement, too, especially when account was taken of something that should never have been connected with this in any way whatsoever; that is what Newfoundland is entitled to as its constitutional right under the terms of union, which has also been mixed up in this formula.
However, it had this wonderful effect, that it really cut New Brunswick down. What was given with the one hand was taken away with the other. For some reason or another New Brunswick was not quite so popular with the present government after June, 1960 as it had been before. So they got another nice little political gimmick worked into this.
8950	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Relations
What is the result? The result, as the minister showed in the tables he put before us on July 11, is that the difference between the old scheme as projected for this year and the new scheme is $17 million approximately. It is costing the treasury $17 million more, and of that $17 million Ontario gains $18 million and the rest of the provinces lose $1 million. Stripped of all the other elements, that is what happened. That is shown in these tables.

maintopic: AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext: But Ontario did not get $100 million.

maintopic: AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Ontario, of course, was very far below what "this man"-to quote the premier of Ontario, as I quoted him before-was going to produce. What did Mr. Frost do? He brought down his budget then, after this scheme was out. He decided the game was up. He brought down his budget and as a memorial to the Diefenbaker-Flem-ing government he established the sales tax. Being a realist and a politician he took good care to point out that it was not his fault that this sales tax was imposed but that the fault lay elsewhere. There is no doubt that as compared with the expectations he was properly entitled to say the fault did lie elsewhere.
Let us look at the result by provinces. British Columbia and Alberta, because they are above the national average, are actually going to get less next year than they are getting this year. Quebec, Manitoba and Saskatchewan will get precisely what they would have got had there been no change whatsoever. New Brunswick gets very little more than it would have got had there been no change-substantially less than a million dollars. The other three Atlantic provinces will get substantially more for the time being. As I say, the one big gainer is Ontario. If the federal government had been prepared to recommend that the provincial government should get a larger share of the tax revenues than they were getting before, if they had felt they could afford to make such an offer, I would not begrudge it to any province on a fair basis, but I do not think anyone could argue that to increase the total amount by $17 million and have $18 million more go to one province is the way to promote that spirit of justice and fair play or that harmony which the Prime Minister promised would be the result of his substitution for the previous administration.
I had hoped-but I have gone on too long -to say something about the attitude of the various provincial premiers toward this proposal. However, most of the provincial premiers are articulate and have made their views known. It is certainly not a happy


chorus that we hear. Not one of them has expressed himself as satisfied. As I said earlier, I do not think that is to be expected. Unlike the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) who were convinced that if they could only sit over there they could make all the premiers happy, I never thought that was possible. I do not think hon. gentlemen who sit on the treasury benches think so now, either. If they do, I advise them to go out and have another interview with Mr. Bennett-if they can find him. There are other premiers whom they could visit. Nothing would give me greater pleasure, for example, than to be able to eavesdrop at the door when the premier of Manitoba is expressing his real views about the way Manitoba has been treated by this government. If there is one government which has loyally, almost slavishly, supported the present government it has been the government of Manitoba, and it has got nothing but kicks, delays and lack of consideration for its pains. Evidently, the view is: you can count on good old Duff. He said "Where Dief goes, Duff will go, too." So there is no need to do anything for him. That seems to be the attitude toward Manitoba and it has been well reflected, I may say, in the treatment of Manitoba in this whole situation. Knowing the way this government approaches all these problems, perhaps one cannot blame them for taking an attitude of that kind toward the government of Saskatchewan, but one would have thought there v/ould have been a little decent feeling toward poor Duff.
There is just one other thing I want to say. The Minister of Finance, speaking on the resolution stage, made one or two of his usual modest and accurate claims in regard to this matter and I think I should say a word or two about that. The minister said, as reported on page 7910 of Hansard:
Although it has greatly improved the financial substance of the present arrangements this government has recognized the weaknesses of the tax rental system which it inherited, both from the provincial and federal standpoint, and has become increasingly convinced of the need for a new approach which would give greater freedom and responsibility to the provincial government and which would be compatible with the constitution.
I may say that this government did not inherit the tax rental system at all. The tax rental system as a system of redistributing revenues was abandoned by the previous government in 1956 in favour of equalization. That was done by the previous government, and no province was financially the loser, whether it had a tax rental agreement or

not. The tax rental system was a pure convenience, and nothing more, from 1957 onward. It was an option which the provinces could take if they wished. No province had to take it in order to get the benefits of the equalization scheme. That is well known to the Minister of Finance, yet he talks jargon like this. Mr. Drew and Mr. Duplessis had a point in 1945 and 1946 when they said that in order to get the benefits of this scheme they were compelled to sign an agreement. But that was all done away with by the previous administration in 1955 and 1956.

Mr. Speaker, it was with some shock and disappointment that this afternoon we found
[Mr. Eicard.l

the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) unwilling to say any more about the dominion-provincial relationship in fiscal matters which had been brought before the house some months ago. For a period of three months no discussion has taken place on this matter. Hon. members were given to believe and I think the Canadian people certainly believed that this was a matter in respect of which there would be considerable give and take, a matter in respect of which there would be negotiation and in respect of which the ideas and concepts of the provincial premiers would be taken into account. It was believed that their arguments and suggestions would be weighed against those of the Minister of Finance and his experts and that out of this amalgam, out of this long term period of thoughtful soul searching a new proposal would be brought forth. And yet, although only two of the ten provinces are going to be helped by this proposal and although seven of the provincial premiers have come out publicly against it, the Minister of Finance chooses to say nothing. One might almost believe that the words which appear at the base of the coat of arms of Canada might no longer be "a mare usque ad mare", but "take it or leave it".
We hoped there would be a wide discussion this afternoon and evening but there will be none and therefore it would seem that we are back at the point where we were last June when we discussed this at the resolution stage.
I am not going to take up the time of the house by reading what provincial premiers have said, by bringing forward statistics, by reading from editorials which appeared in newspapers across the nation. I simply wish to point out the three great principles which we believe these proposals violate. First, they will not over the years give provinces sufficient money to carry out their constitutional tasks. Second, they will not ensure that an individual living in any part of Canada will have equal opportunity for all the various services with every other individual in any other part of Canada. Finally, they are a negation of the principle that the dominion government must assume responsibility for fiscal and monetary planning at the national level which will ensure a full employment society and a better way of life.
As the Prime Minister took us back through history this afternoon and recounted with some validity, although I must say it was a misuse of history to some extent, that the party now in power had always had progressive views in the area of railways-as I say, it had a certain measure of validity-I could not help thinking of that area where the first

prime minister of this nation certainly had one blind spot, and that was in the area of federalism because Sir John A. Macdonald saw the provinces as merely large municipalities. Indeed, Sir John A. Macdonald would have been just as happy to see no provinces at all, no federal system at all, but rather a unitary state set up within the boundaries of this country. As a result, I think we have a kind of historic blind spot when it comes to dealing with the problem of federal-provincial relationships on the part of this government.
We in this group believe that there is a role for the provinces, and it is more than simply accepting conditional grants; it is more than simply carrying out the administration of federally initiated programs; it is more than simply a level of government which transfers money from above to below. We believe that the provinces can play a very dynamic role. In fact one might even suggest that the length of time we have sat in this chamber would indicate that perhaps the dominion government has bitten off more than it can chew. We have debated many things which will be redebated in all the provincial legislatures. While the provincial legislatures sit perhaps eight, ten weeks or 12 weeks, we sit from November to the following September. One might wonder whether a redivision not only of money but also of time, energy and talk might well be one subject to which we could put our minds.
To return to the first point, we believe that the twentieth century and all the problems of the twentieth century in an industrial society demand to quite an extent monetary and fiscal planning at the national level, which may not be enough. We are handicapped by giving over taxation responsibilities to the provincial governments. We feel that there must be some form of anti-cyclical budgeting. This is, of course, what we have been appealing for in vain over the last two or three years. But now that the recession is over this is the time when we shall need, and need very badly, what might be called a slowdown, possibly by means of fiscal and monetary policy, to stop a galloping inflation or a galloping expansion, and a realization that fiscal and monetary policy at the national level can accelerate our economy if such a recession should occur again. We feel that by giving over these powers in certain areas, as has been done by this system, the dominion government will be in a very serious position when it comes to adjusting the economy of this nation and finding a pattern whereby this nation's economy can find solutions in the coming days. This is the first reason and the first principle which we feel these dominion-provincial agreements violate.

The second, of course, and perhaps the most important is that of equalization. In spite of all the protests of the Minister of Finance and his experts, the form of equalization which is suggested by this system is not equalization at all, as has been stated already. He that hath will be given more.
It must be recognized that in a country the size of Canada, with its tremendous differences in resources, with the effect that national policies, tariffs and transportation will have on various people in various sections, some adjustment must be made. We believe that the adjustment of equalization that has been established over the last 20 years or so is one of the most valuable contributions that this nation has made to the whole concept of federalism throughout the world.
We believe-as I am sure all hon. members believe-that a man in no matter what part of Canada should have the same opportunity for the same kind of health services; that any young person should have the same opportunity for education; that all the opportunities for progress should be the same in each province. We believe that this change in the equalization system will not bring this about. All must share in the nation's wealth. This is where we feel this system very sadly indeed negates what has gone before. Surely, Mr. Speaker, during the 1930's this nation fought its way through with a constitutional division of powers and fiscal powers which made it very difficult indeed to deal with the unemployment and other dreadful problems of that era.
The fathers of confederation knew nothing of the difficulties of the twentieth century; but at the end of that period we came to a solution, and the Rowell-Sirois report stands as one of the great symbols of Canada's looking ahead at that point. Unfortunately the second world war came along just at the time when Canada would have taken a major step in the direction of equalization. But at least during the war we did make, I think, very important plans to adjust our policies to give a high degree of equalization.
The Rowell-Sirois report, of course, expected experts to be able to base the equalization on need. Whether that is possible I do not know. Whether we can determine the need of Newfoundland fishermen with respect to that of say the western farmer, and that of the British Columbia lumberman with that of the Ontario labourer. I do not know. I am not sure whether that can be done. But surely we have been moving in that direction, a direction which I do not think anyone in Canada wants to have reversed. That was the watershed of dominion-provincial relations, and it was with the greatest sadness and the

Dominion-Provincial Relations greatest concern that this party has seen a reversal of that trend since that most important watershed. We believe that it will have the most serious effects as the smaller provinces, or the less wealthy provinces, are forced to raise their taxes in areas which will be unpopular. We know, Mr. Speaker, that this is not a popular subject anyway. Dominion-provincial relations always are politically unpopular because they come right down to the pocketbook of the individual Canadian; they come right down to the most unpopular task which any government has to do, and that is collect taxes. But surely, in the enlightened age in which we hope we live this should not stand in our way in continuing the trend which has been moving in the last years toward greater and greater equalization.
As the poor provinces increase their corporation taxes, their succession duties, their sales taxes and so on, industry will move to those provinces which can afford not to increase them. We will have more concentration of industry in the rich provinces and the rich provinces will get richer and the poor provinces will become poorer in spite of any protests in the opposite direction. This is the second reason why this party believes that this is a backward step. We believe also that it will create a jungle of taxation. Someone called it the jungle of the 1930's.
We do believe that without at least some order in the tax collecting policy of this country, there will be chaos. We feel that this would be most unfortunate and most unjust.
The third and final reason we feel that this is a negation of government responsibility is that over the years the provinces will lose their power to carry out the real objectives of their existence. We deny that the system will provide more money to the provinces. The Minister of Finance says that in the last few years of recession the opportunities for taxation have decreased and so the opportunities of the federal powers to give money to the provinces have also decreased. Surely, Mr. Speaker, this situation exists as well in so far as the provinces are concerned. No doubt the provinces have had to increase their taxes and apply sales taxes or gasoline taxes whereas, according to the Minister of Finance, the federal government has been able to lower its taxes. The burden on the provinces, therefore, is even greater. We would hope that this government is not now, at this stage of its administration, deciding we are going to have a continued recession and that this
will continue to be a problem over the years in terms of adjusting our relationship with the provinces.
We feel, and I think very properly, that for these reasons the democratic party cannot support this particular proposal. We feel that it will emphasize the disparity in the levels of prosperity in the various provinces. For example, the 5 per cent increase will yield $2.50 per capita in Ontario but will yield only 60 cents per capita in Newfoundland. The Minister of Finance has decided he will say no more. He indicates that he will stand where he did last June. We have put our position and we feel this is unfair to the provinces. We feel it destroys equalization and, finally, we feel it is a negation of the responsibilities of the government. We cannot, therefore, possibly support this measure.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great attention to the remarks of the learned opposition members on this matter, and I was more particularly amused by the lengthy tirades of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill).
It is always exhilarating to hear him discourse because I might say that not only in his speeches, but also in his general behaviour, he seems to have the lyrical, and even the romantic touch.
He mentioned, for instance, that he would very much like to eavesdrop at the door when the premier of Manitoba and the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) met with regard to those problems. But what was he doing when he was an active member of the former Liberal government?
Now, did he eavesdrop on the recriminations which not only the Canadian taxpayers, but the spokesmen of all provinces came to voice here in Ottawa, or did he rather at that time-as he seems unaware of such complaints-enjoy walking the famous dog Pat in the enchanting lanes of Ottawa?
We recall that, since 1945, the unyielding and centralizing attitude of the former Liberal government gave rise to many protests throughout the country. For instance, you only have to look briefly through some statements of provincial premiers, of which, to my mind, the oddest is one made in 1956 by the premier of Newfoundland, Mr. Smallwood, who, himself a Liberal threatened, under Liberal rule, to dissociate himself from the Canadian federation if Ottawa persisted in denying him fair treatment.

In 1956, Mr. Frost also stated the following:
That is the same government as the one which resorts to mean tactics in a field of taxation that belongs to Ontario as much as to Ottawa.
Here, in Ontario, in order to make ends meet, we must subject our people to a form of double taxation. It is a shame that things should come to this, at the very time when Nova Scotia announces a deficit and when New Brunswick is faced with financial problems.
During the same period, Mr. Fines, the provincial treasurer of Saskatchewan, had this to say:
The share of tax revenues allowed to the provinces by Ottawa, under the new agreements, is entirely inadequate to enable them to meet the costs of services of provincial and local governments.
Mr. Patterson, the treasurer of New Brunswick, concluded his budget speech by stating:
The basis of provincial taxes is too narrow to meet the increasing demands made upon the province and its municipalities in peacetime.
Not only did the previous Liberal government thrust on the people of Canada and the provincial governments intransigent and centralizing points of view, but in the application of the tax and allowances sharing, it acted quite unjustly, as it distributed the money according to a principle that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate still wants to uphold today.
We also remember what happened in 1956 when certain provinces that had received too much money from Ottawa were forced, after having started to spend their provincial budgets, to return certain amounts to the federal government. Those poorer provinces are Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Manitoba and Saskatchewan. On the other hand, the richer provinces-of course, they had received less- received more afterwards, even during the administration of their budgets for that year. All this shows that the complicated system initiated by the Liberal government had caused glaring injustice to the provinces and created confusion in public administration. It is for that reason that the people of Canada, conscious of the turn of events, acted positively in 1957 by showing the government that had initiated those unacceptable measures that it was time to come back to confederation, the sound ideas of the Canadian constitution, the British North America Act of 1867.
The new formula is an effort towards decentralization. In fact, it is under a false principle that one government collects taxes that are spent by another government. These 90205-6-565J
Dominion-Provincial Relations are not new statements, and I mean to stay above party politics. In fact, it was Sir Wilfrid Laurier who enunciated that principle in 1887 when he said that one government should not collect taxes to be spent by another government.
In 1930, the late Mr. Mackenzie King recalled the same principle. He then pointed out that it was a faulty principle which made it possible for one government to collect taxes and for another government, to spend the money through subsidies; however, this is what the previous Liberal government did progressively from 1945 to 1957. It seems that after 1945, the late Mr. Mackenzie King had forgotten the sincerity of his reference and had even opened the door for his successors to continue in this anticonstitutional direction.
The new scheme brought down by the present Progressive Conservative government is an effort towards decentralization. It seeks to let the federal government collect its own taxes and to let the provinces recover their fiscal freedom and receive their share of the taxes. It is therefore a return to the con-federative deal, to our Canadian constitution, for the Canadian provinces have powers which are eloquently set out in the British North America Act, especially in clause 92 thereof.
In fact, what matters is not only to have the powers, but also the financial ways and means required to exercise them; that is why the terms of clause 92 of the British North America Act, besides allocating the powers to the provinces, provide the financial means required for their application.
This new scheme is a return to the spirit of the Canadian constitution. The provinces will thus progressively recover their fiscal freedom. In this regard, may I briefly quote from the views of Mr. Gerard Filion, editor of the newspaper Le Devoir, as set out in an editorial which was published on February 25, 1961. This is what he had to say:
From a purely constitutional point of view, the Diefenbaker proposals are a definite improvement. The provinces, in any case those which value their freedom, should be satisfied.
A little farther, in the same editorial, Mr. Filion continues:
If the provinces want to recover some ground, they must not be content with claiming more money from Ottawa, but rather offer to accept greater responsibilities.
That is precisely the nature, the substance and the purpose of this new formula, to give the provinces of Canada their fiscal freedom. Of course, it is not complete, it is not perfect,
8956	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Relations but it is a step in the right direction. It is a lead, an open door away from centralization; it is a decentralizing action aimed at giving back to the provinces the fiscal freedom which they clamoured for, and, although some did not clamour for it, deep down they have always longed to be given back their responsibilities.
So what is the substance of that formula? After March 31, 1962, Ottawa will no longer pay any fiscal allowances to the provinces, but the provinces will be able to levy themselves, or through Ottawa, free of charge, their own share of the three fields of direct taxation.
Although the federal government agreed to reduce its share in the three fields of direct taxation on the basis of specific amounts each year during the next tax-sharing period, it volunteered to levy provincial taxes in those fields at any rate of taxation established by the provinces.
This means that the provinces will be able to decide on taxation rates superior or inferior to the federal withdrawal in those fields. The only reservation imposed by the federal government is that the provincial tax rate shall be determined according to the same definition of taxable revenue as under the federal Income Tax Act.
The federal government agreed to reduce its personal income tax rate by 16 per cent for the taxation year 1962, and by another 1 per cent each year until the federal withdrawal reaches 20 per cent. With regard to the corporation income tax, the federal government agreed to continue reducing its own corporation income tax by 9 per cent of the taxable corporation revenue. It is to be noted that the federal withdrawal in the corporation income tax field is not 9 per cent of the federal levies on corporation income, but 9 per cent of the taxable corporation income.
As the current federal corporation income tax currently levied-with the exception of the old age security tax-is 47 per cent for corporations with a taxable income over $35,000 and 18 per cent for corporations with a lesser income, the federal corporation income tax is about 41 per cent of the total taxable corporation income. If the federal withdrawal of 9 per cent is expressed as a percentage of the current federal income tax levy, rather than as a percentage of taxable revenue, the federal withdrawal will be approximately 22 per cent. In the first year of the new arrangements, the federal gov-vernment itself will levy 84 per cent, 78 per cent, and 50 per cent of its current revenue in those three fields and 80 per cent, 78 per cent and 50 percent in the last year of the new agreements.


The federal government has also agreed to maintain the equalization principle, but on a wider basis in accordance with the national average. Instead of equalizing payments to the provinces until they reach the yield of those three direct taxation fields in the two provinces where that yield was highest per capita, the federal government now offers the provinces an equalization payment equal to the difference between the yield of those three taxation fields per capita in each province, and the national average of the per capita yield of those three taxes, as well as an amount equal to the per capita amount by which provincial per capita revenue from natural resources has fallen below national average yield of provincial revenue from natural resources. In order to determine the amount to be attributed to the equalization factor based on natural resources, provincial revenue from natural resources per capita was established by taking 50 per cent of a moving scale for three years of provincial revenues from that source.
It has been decided to equalize provincial revenues from natural resources at 50 per cent of a moving scale over three years, for several reasons. As the provincial tax rates on natural resources and revenues derived from them vary from one province to the other and from one resource to the other, it was thought proper to consider those differences by using in the equalization formula 50 per cent rather than 100 per cent of revenues from resources. The three year average was used to avoid the marked differences sometimes shown in that source of revenue due to natural disasters or to the sale of resources.
In addition to equalization based on the national average, all the provinces are assured that they will not get less under the new tax rates of 16-9-50, 17-9-50, 18-9-50, etc., above and over equalization payments based on the national average than they would have received with the normal tax rates of 13-9-50, with equalization based on the average of the two provinces where yield was the highest in the previous year or on the average for the last two years of the current agreements, whichever may be the highest. In addition, the provinces which are under the national average according to the new formula have a guarantee that they will never get less in normal tax yield and equalization based on the national average than they would have received in the same year through an extrapolation of the agreements now in force.
This is the substance of this formula now before the house and examined from several angles.

It is obvious that this formula must show its worth. We must let it be implemented for some time, but we can already rest assured that it represents a real effort of this Conservative administration to decentralize and to gradually restore to the provinces their tax fields and their fiscal responsibilities. For we still want to believe in the existence and actuality of the constitution of 1867, we still want to have faith in the benefits of Canadian federalism. It must be recognized that this Canadian federalism of ours is based on an association of autonomous governments which in their activities, as described in articles 91 and 92 of the constitution, have their own powers and also their own means of financing in order to exercise such powers. And Canadian federalism clearly establishes that the various governments shall not be subjected one to another, but so co-ordinated. Those various governments, due to that federalist character of our constitution, must co-operate in common schemes, as it is stipulated, for instance, in article 95, as regards agriculture and immigration.
The new formula seeks a reconciliation after so many years of separation, after so many years of dislocation, for if we look back over the years we find that an agreement between various governments, in terms of our current economy, presents to our governments problems that are different from those of 1867. Because of particular circumstances resulting from an economic depression, or a war, governments have made concessions to each other; but after having benefited by concessions, the Liberal government maintained its hold, continued war in the fiscal field up to 1957, instead of realizing that the fiscal and economic war was over since 1945. Some have taken advantage of the confusion that happened in fiscal relations between the governments to interfere in fiscal fields that they did not own. The federal government took possession of taxation fields like personal income tax and corporation income tax and succession duties. Of course, it was not directly and absolutely forbidden by the constitution to impose direct taxation, because those three taxes I just mentioned are direct taxes; but the constitution states quite clearly that the federal government cannot levy taxes in those fields when the taxes are to be used for provincial purposes. What was wrong in the Liberal government's approach, was to seek to follow a centralizing policy with paternalism by distributing to the provinces certain amounts of money that it collected in fields that belonged to the provinces.
Dominion-Provincial Relations
There are also provinces which, during those years have entered indirect taxation fields, while those fields under section 91, paragraph 3, belonged to the federal government.
In this last instance, I mean indirect taxes on retail sales, taxes on security transfers, on meals, on theater tickets and on gasoline and oil. Those indirect taxes collected by the provinces, were called direct taxes by the privy council because they were collected directly from the final consumer without including them in the initial price.
It must be remembered that during all those constitutional years existed such chaos and difficulties, the strait-jacket mentioned tonight by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill). The result of those trends is that various governments intruded into taxation fields not clearly devolving upon them under the Canadian constitution. In addition the Liberal government was claiming unflinchingly for paternalistic reasons that it had to levy taxes, and through subsidies let provincial governments spend those amounts. That was meant to destroy the principle of responsible government which we have enjoyed for many years, because a responsible government, under the very spirit of our constitution, is the one which levies the taxes and spends them. It is accountable to the Canadian people for its tax collections and that responsibility does not devolve on any other government.
I welcome this new formula put forward by the Progressive Conservative government.
One might say, like the Conservative party of 1867 which was at the origin of the Canadian confederation, that it is the Conservative party of 1961 which, after so many difficulties, such confusion, and despite the acrobatics of the previous Liberal administration, makes serious, commendable and sincere efforts to return to the spirit of confederation.
Mr. Speaker, the legislation brought forward before the House of Commons as well as the topics discussed last year by the interested parties at the dominion-provincial conferences show that we are at a turning point of our constitutional venture, for we shall soon bring our constitution back home, and we shall then be able to amend it with the consent of the provinces. I take this opportunity to offer my warmest congratulations to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) for the efforts he has made, in conjunction

Dominion-Provincial Relations with all the provincial ministers to repatriate our Canadian constitution, so that we shall be able to say, not only in principle but also in fact, that we have at long last a sovereign constitution, that we are able to amend without having to refer to any other country. By amending our constitution, I do not mean that we shall upset it, but rather clarify it, define it in clearer terms, and correct the incongruities brought about through the years by governmental practices and interventions.
In this context, it can be said that the present Progressive Conservative government presides over this wonderful trend towards the very spirit of the confederation deal, for if the present central government needs resources and particular revenues to meet its ever-increasing commitments, it nevertheless remains deeply human, and understands that the autonomous and sovereign provinces must preserve their economic independence by maintaining the fields of taxation granted to them by the constitution. The passing of the legislation now before us is the only way to achieve this, and I shall be glad to vote for it because it opens the door to the confederation deal of 1867.
That is why the province of Quebec is in favour of it. She will not be content with aleatory and illusory powers; she wants financial powers so that the province can carry on its responsibilities.
In practice when the representatives of the provinces and of the dominion government meet together to amend the constitution, adjustments will be brought about. But there is a field where Quebec will allow no change whatsoever, that is, the field of higher education, whose importance is clearly set out in clause 93 of our constitution, which grants to the provinces exclusive jurisdiction over this matter.
Without any reflection on the approach of other provinces-we, French Canadians from the province of Quebec, respect the views of the other provinces, and that is probably part of our worth, for we love our country and have great respect for the views of our fellow citizens-we keep a jealous watch over our own prerogatives. That is why the province of Quebec remains steadfast in its attitude, no matter which party is in power. Whether it be at the time of the Hon. Messrs. Taschereau, Duplessis, Sauve or Barrette- and even under Mr. Jean Lesage-the premiers of Quebec unfailingly voice the intent and desire of a whole people living in this comer of our Canadian land, to retain absolute control in the field of education, for,

while we respect and admire other cultures, we are proud of our own, we want to remain masters of that culture, and direct it in our own way.
In order to do that, we need financial means; that explains the stand taken by the province of Quebec. Regardless of political parties, nothing is bad or evil and it is in that spirit that everything is done.
We respect the views of the other provinces, of our fellow citizens, but we demand that others understand us so that with the assistance of the present government, we may recover progressively the prerogatives which are dear to us in that field.
Last year, the present government reached an agreement with the late Hon. Mr. Sauve on a formula with respect to university grants. That was a step in the right direction and it enabled the province to collect the money which had accumulated.
We must always keep in mind that when the federal government takes a step, it must not favour only one province, but must introduce legislation which is suitable for all the provinces of Canada. It was understood that under that formula, the corporation income tax was to be raised by 1 per cent and that in return the corporations would benefit from an equal rebate with respect to the federal corporation income tax. Recently, I read in the newspapers-I did not have the chance to read the official correspondence-that the premier of the province of Quebec has refused to accept that formula on the grounds that he would accept the formula if it did not require the provinces to waive a certain surplus.
I would not say that the present premier of the province of Quebec is entirely wrong, but what I hold against him is that the formula in question, even though it was not perfect, was a step in the right direction since it was most advantageous to the universities of the province, while the latter were still getting direct assistance from the provincial government.
Hon. Mr. Lesage is now closing the door, probably for mere political considerations. I would not want to impute any motives to him, but I find his attitude most amazing. The autonomy he advocates is a negative one. He has not suggested any other formula, he has just closed the door and complicated matters. I wish he would follow the example of his predecessor, the Hon. Paul Sauve, and come up with an adequate formula of his choice.

I am sure that the present federal government will give close consideration to that formula. I hope the premier will act immediately so that the province may not suffer from any delay.
As for myself, I should like to make four suggestions to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in this field of education. I suggest:
1.	That this government publicly state its intention of considering as coming exclusively within the provincial jurisdiction all representations to increase the payments now made by the government of Canada, either to provincial governments or to teaching institutions, by way of grants or assistance of any kind to education at all levels;
2.	That the government recognize the principle that, in due time, the control and distribution of the various kinds of assistance to education at present provided by the federal government should be returned to the provinces;
3.	That the solution to the problem be sought by possible inclusion of the federal educational grants in the equalization payments provided the provinces under the present tax arrangements, and that both these payments be amalgamated and considered together when the renewal of tax-sharing arrangements is discussed;
4.	That the foregoing be immediately implemented as far as university grants are concerned with the understanding, if need be, that the federal government shall be prepared-unless otherwise decided by the fiscal conference-to increase each year the equalization payments by the sum by which the university grants were to be increased, that is $1.50 per capita according to the increase in population.
