speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill raises the question of federal-provincial tax relations. It is a complicated problem and I shall try to deal with it in the most objective way possible.
A moment ago, I listened with great interest to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) who indicated that the new formula which forms the basis of this bill infringes the principle of the legislation introduced by the Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent's administration and that the application of that formula will be detrimental to the great majority of the provinces.
The first point I wish to make is that, by introducing this bill, the Conservative government admits its inability to find a basis of agreement which would be more beneficial to the provinces than the previous one. The
Dominion-Provincial Relations government must be blamed, not only for the failure of the last federal-provincial conference, but especially for having held out, even before the conference even took place, promises which they knew or should have known they could not keep.
Speaking of promises, they were of two kinds. As a matter of fact, in the province of Quebec, our Conservative friends had come out against the equalization system as being contrary to the B.N.A. Act while, in the nine other provinces, the Prime Minister pledged to preserve it intact, as witness these lines from the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix for February 14, 1958, where in the Prime Minister is reported as stating:
(Text):
I stated that the equalization principle would be preserved. I say it again, and I repeat it now. The principle will be put into effect.
(Translation):
That is not what our friends, the Conservatives, were saying in the province of Quebec. At any rate, in both cases, this bill proves that the promises made in 1958 have been repudiated. The taxation fields have not been abandoned as the Quebec Conservatives promised it and the equalization formula has not been left unchanged as the Prime Minister had guaranteed.
Speaking of equalization, I feel it would be a good thing at this point to quote once more what Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent said, as reported in Hansard for January 12, 1956:
After examining many possible plans, we came to the conclusion that the most generally acceptable means of bridging this gap in Canada between the costs of essential provincial services and the wide variations in the tax potentials available to the provincial governments, would be to develop a pattern of tax equalization payments from the federal to the provincial governments.
With his customary modesty, Mr. St. Laurent went on:
We have never contended that these agreements were a perfect answer to the problems in our fiscal relationships but that is the best formula that has been devised yet-and the steps we are taking-will be conducive to the growth and development of all the provinces and of that spirit of solidarity from one ocean to the other.
The aim pursued by Mr. St. Laurent and his government was therefore to reduce the gap between the incomes which the various provinces derived from taxes so that all provinces and all taxpayers would become equal partners in the confederation.
It must be recognized, I think, that this formula has stood the test of time. In the critical post-war years, it enabled the provinces, which were faced with expansion prob-

Dominion-Provincial Relations lems, to develop more harmoniously and it reduced considerably the gap between the provinces' income.
Thanks to that formula, citizens of all provinces enjoyed the benefits of comparable services.
There is another advantage which is far from being the least. By removing the inequalities which were prejudicial to the poorer provinces, the St. Laurent formula largely contributed to a better understanding of national unity.
It will be recalled that the equalization principle was denounced as being contrary to the spirit and letter of confederation.
I should like to deal immediately with a misrepresentation which was repeated tonight by the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard), a myth which our Conservative friends have kept alive in the province of Quebec and which has no foundation either in law or in history. It was said repeatedly that the equalization formula was the result of a centralization which was contrary to the spirit and letter of the constitution. Consequently, it will be necessary for me, I think, to go back briefly to the sources. With the help of historical data, I will prove that not only were subsidies an integral part of the pact of 1867 and-I do mean an integral part of the 1867 pact, but that the payment of those subsidies was a paramount condition to the entry into confederation of lower Canada and the maritimes.
On page 5290 of volume 3 of Hansard of 1906, we can read section 64 of the Quebec resolutions, outlining the following proposal. I quote:
In consideration of the transfer to the general parliament of the powers of taxation, an annual grant in aid of each province shall be made, equal to 80 cents per head of the population-
And, as recorded on page 5291 of Hansard of March 25, 1907, the then prime minister, the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, stated:
But it is also a matter of history that if the resolutions were passed in a certain form, if the allowance to the provinces were arranged in a certain way, the reason, the paramount reason, was that without such an enactment and such an allowance the provinces would not have consented to enter confederation.
Now, here is a statement of policy, made in 1865, by Mr. Brown, one of the fathers of confederation:
I do not think I am being indiscreet in saying that, at the conference, I was most vocal in asking that all local expenses be paid by local governments through direct taxation; and that there were liberal-minded men, coming from all parts of the provinces, who would have liked
[Mr. Deschatelets.l

nothing better than to see such a proposal accepted. But, Mr. Speaker, there was an obstacle, an obstacle we often meet in this world, and that obstacle amounted to this: the impossibility in which we were to have the idea accepted. We would not have been able to rally the members of the conference, neither those of the existing provincial legislatures.
I am afraid, our friends in Lower Canada constitutionally object to direct taxation.
And, as can be seen on the same page, Sir Wilfrid Laurier added the following statement:
This is conclusive evidence. Lower Canada would never have entered confederation, if, by that very fact, it had been forced to resort to direct taxation to levy the required sums for the management of its local business. The same state of mind prevailed in the Maritime provinces. Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island would never have agreed to the federal pact if they had to resort to direct taxation as a consequence.
Well, Mr. Speaker, those are statements that need no comment. And I want to support those statements by quoting indisputable figures. For the fiscal year 1867-1868, 54 per cent of the total provincial revenue was derived from subsidies by the Canadian government. From 1868 to 1888, that percentage varied from year to year between 42 and 57 per cent. In the period from 1888 to 1909, the percentage of subsidies paid to the provinces by the federal government varied between 29 and 37 per cent, after which they gradually decreased down to the depression years, from 1930 to 1935, whereas in 1955, that percentage reached 46 per cent, and subsequently decreased.
Now, in the case of Quebec, we find that, for the fiscal year 1867-1868, 59.67 per cent of the total revenue of that province was derived from federal subsidies. During the first ten years of confederation, that percentage reached an average of 46 per cent. In the first 25 years after confederation, the percentage for Quebec was 37.5 per cent.
Well, Mr. Speaker, those figures are part of this country's history. I trust they will be read again and considered by our Conservative friends in Quebec who will then be able to revise some of the conclusions reached in their speeches with regard to federal-provincial fiscal matters. It is therefore a well established fact that, during the lifetime of the fathers of confederation, the provinces lived for the greater part on federal subsidies and that, moreover, neither Quebec nor the maritime provinces would have entered confederation without a guarantee that those subsidies would be paid by the federal government.

-of the system of grants to the provinces; quite the contrary, it is indeed to reply to several fallacious and erroneous arguments that are used too often to serve certain purposes.
One thing is sure though, it is that the fathers of confederation have accepted and the provinces have demanded in order to join the confederation, an equitable system of revenues, apart from direct taxation, to be able to efficiently fulfil their constitutional obligations.
Dominion-Provincial Relations
In the light of what I have just said, it is quite obvious that the equalization formula of the St. Laurent government was not contrary to the confederation, but more than this government's formula it encouraged solidarity between the provinces, solidarity that is vital to this great federal family.
Mr. Speaker, the new formula, which is the basis of this bill, is inferior to the former one and destroys the principle of revenue equalization because it does not seek to treat all provinces on an equal basis.
At the resolution stage, on July 11 last, we wondered on what basis the Minister of Finance made the following statement. I quote from page 7910 of Hansard:
The government has materially increased the return to the provinces from the existing tax sharing arrangements.
And we recall the lack of enthusiasm of the premiers of the various provinces and their expressed dissatisfaction. In fact, in February, the premier of British Columbia said:
I am disappointed that my province will not receive equalization payments.
On February 27, the premier of Alberta said that he was disappointed by this new arrangement.
The treasurer of Saskatchewan said that his province would not receive the amounts that it would have under the existing agreements.
The premier of Alberta said on April 8 that the new agreement presented certain features that he approved, but he added nevertheless that it was disappointing to see that his province would not receive any immediate increase.
The premier of Ontario said that this formula did not provide for his province anything like the $150 million additional yearly revenues he sought to obtain during the two day conference. And he added that his last resort was to levy new taxes.
We recall these words of the premier of Quebec:
Equalization has just been killed.
The New Brunswick premier said that the new fiscal proposals "would cause enduring harm". The premiers of Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland said they were satisfied and they accepted the formula but with some reservations.
That is how the new formula based on the average national revenues, on equalization, not from the top but from the middle, was received by the provinces.
After four years of conferences and negotiations, this cannot be called a great

Dominion-Provincial Relations success. In fact, it is a resounding failure if we look at the promises that were made. However, we have cause for comfort because the Conservative government has invited the provinces to levy additional revenues themselves by collecting their own taxes. As if that right had not always existed. That is what the province of Ontario has already done, because the provincial tax which became effective on September 1 is the first tangible result of the fiscal federal-provincial failure. And it is after the provinces had been invited to resort to taxes that the Secretary of State (Mr. Dorion) stated recently in a flight of oratory: "This is the end of limitations; it is a reversion to the spirit and the letter of the constitution".
I showed a moment ago that this assertion is historically and legally erroneous and unfounded.
When one thinks that the Canadian taxpayer is already overtaxed, this is an invitation which does not constitute a very glittering policy for a government on the eve of an election.
If the government had been consistent or had fulfilled the promises made in Quebec by its candidates, it would have given the various fields of taxation back to the provinces. On the contrary, since 1958, it has clung to them more than any other previous government. This government has piled up deficits, expenditures, loans and high interests.
It must be remembered that in 1958 we had a $38.5 million deficit, $609,500,000 in 1959, $413 million in 1960, $300 million in 1961 and in 1962, according to the Canadian tax foundation estimate, Canada will incur a deficit of approximately $700 million.
From 1957 to 1961, the unemployment insurance fund was drained of approximately $900 million.
During the same period, $165 million were used out of the national defence special fund.
Those amounts total $3,126 million, or an additional debt of $750 for each Canadian family and it is in that financially stifling atmosphere that this government urges the provinces to accept its invitation to levy additional taxes in their own jurisdiction.
With all these facts, I feel that this Conservative government now levies within the provinces a higher ratio of taxes than any previous government and I am tempted to ask myself: If this is centralization, where are the centralizers, if they are not sitting to your right, Mr. Speaker?
I stated that those fiscal proposals were made by this government to the provinces

which asked for a revision and a reconsideration thereof, but all the attempts to renew discussions were coolly turned down.
Let us admit that today we are voting for a five year failure. The dies are cast.
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish, in the course of my remarks, to limit myself to criticism of the government. I should now like to consider the problem in order to facilitate its solution. I sincerely believe that the tax collection agreements with the provincial governments are complex because we have there a problem which cannot be dealt with satisfactorily before the major problem is solved; and the major problem is the redistribution of taxation powers and the respective responsibilities of the federal and the provincial governments.
Thus, it seems that the time has come to reconsider the Canadian constitution in the light of its 94 years of existence, and that the problems which arise here, in Canada, in 1961 will have to be reconsidered.
To that purpose, we must first reach an agreement with the provinces about a method of amending our constitution. That is the first step to take. Then, the government and the provinces, around a conference table, will have to determine a redistribution, as accurate and flexible as possible, of the powers of taxation and the respective administrative responsibilities. Surely, this will be delicate and difficult work. It will be a matter of putting back the rights and privileges of 1867 in a more up-to-date framework, yet preserving and strengthening if possible all the clauses and powers pertaining to the rights, privileges and autonomy of the provinces.
That is, I think, the main problem that arises in Canada today. It will have to be solved without delay so that the development and economic and industrial growth of the provinces will not be hindered.
To deal with this important problem, it has become necessary for the government to establish a department of federal-provincial affairs. 1 believe each province should set up such a department. Quebec already has shown the way in this connection. It would then be the responsibility of these ministers, through continuous contacts and consideration of problems we have in common with the provinces, to prepare and submit a report which, in a year or two, could become the second constitutional charter of Canada.
If such a work were undertaken now, there would be no reason for not finding a solution within the next two or three years. By adopting such a method, the arrangement contained in the bill before the house could easily be limited to two or three years instead of extending to five.

For it is my feeling that, within a year or two, we will have an election and it is a distinct possibility that those who are now at the left of the Speaker will be the ones called upon to decide, within two years, on the constitution to be given this country.
Mr. Speaker, when I said a moment ago that the time had come to take a second look at taxation powers, I had in mind the attitude of the government of the province of Quebec on joint plans, which are closely related to taxation powers.
It will be remembered that in La Reforme of June 24, 1961, Mr. Lesage had this to say:
The sooner we can substitute to the joint plans our own plans based on revenue back from Ottawa, the better it will be for us.
he Devoir, on Tuesday, September 26, 1961, quoted the Quebec minister of natural resources, Mr. Rene Levesque, as saying:
It would be better if joint programs disappeared gradually.
I should like, Mr. Speaker, to comment on those two statements. I wish to make it clear at the outset that there is no contradiction between the stand taken by the Quebec government and that of the St. Laurent government which introduced the joint programs which were so beneficial to all Canadians, whether it be hospital insurance, the trans-Canada highway, or the roads to resources program. In my opinion, the attitude taken by the Quebec provincial government is what we have always considered as positive autonomy, because even though Quebec expresses that wish, nevertheless, until the powers are redistributed, it accepts all the money which is spent under those joint programs, for the simple reason that that money belongs partly to the taxpayers of all the provinces-Quebec taxpayers like all the others-who are entitled to benefit from all possible services. Those services they are paying for through their taxes, whether it be to the federal or to the provincial government.
There is no point in comparing that attitude to that of Mr. Duplessis of whom it was said that he was practising a negative autonomy. And now that the Duplessis regime is a thing of the past, and that we now have a Liberal government in Quebec, we can, by simply comparing, determine the advantages of a positive autonomy policy over a negative policy. Mr. Duplessis stood for the return of taxation rights but because of his failure to take any initiative, by systematically turning down-

Hon. members will remember that at the last federal-provincial conference he attended he stated: "It is cash we want".
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will remember that in the strictly federal field, Mr. St. Laurent's administration obtained the power to amend our constitution in this country in 1950. For the reasons we know, it was impossible to proceed with the provinces and amend our constitution here in Canada as far as provincial and joint matters are concerned. I wish to emphasize-the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) has already done so-the remarkable work of the provincial minister of youth, Mr. Gerin-Lajoie, whose work, initiative and knowledge of constitutional matters enabled us to expect a solution in the near future.
Mr. Speaker, to sum up I would suggest this to the government first of all, the immediate creation of a department of federal-provincial affairs; second, obtaining the power to amend the constitution in this country in joint and provincial matters at the earliest opportunity; third, immediate consideration of taxation powers and mutual responsibility between the central government and the provinces, in order to bring the constitution up to date for solving the problems arising in Canada today. But, until those measures are taken, I subscribe to the remarks of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), and I ask this government to come back to the formula of the St. Laurent government with regard to equalization payments, because if the bill remains in its present form, I shall have to vote against it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have had a very interesting debate on the subject matter of Bill No. C-122. As hon. members know, this bill was introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in this house on July 12, just prior to the summer recess. In the ensuing weeks most of us have had an opportunity of studying the bill, reading the speeches of the various premiers during the series of conferences and trying to familiarize ourselves with the details of this involved piece of legislation.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
It is common knowledge that since confederation federal governments have always been obliged to lend financial aid and assistance to the provinces of Canada. This aid invariably took the form of special or conditional grants. In fact, prior to 1942 we had no evidence at all of unconditional grants. In 1941 Mr. Ilsley, the then minister of finance in his budget speech indicated that, whether or not there was an agreement, the provinces would have to vacate the personal and corporate fields of taxation for the duration of the war and one year thereafter. Consequently, in 1942 this House of Commons passed for the first time a bill authorizing unconditional grants and entitled the Dominion-Provincial Taxation Agreement Act. In 1947 a new bill was introduced and passed known as the Dominion-Provincial Tax Rental Agreements Act. It remained in effect for a period of five years and was replaced in 1952 by the second tax rental agreement act, namely the Tax Rental Agreements Act, 1952.
In 1942 the province of New Brunswick received the sum of $4.2 million. In 1947, under the first tax rental agreements act, the province of New Brunswick received a total of $13.3 million, $8 million from tax rental and approximately $5 million from equalization payments. During the 1952 to 1957 agreements New Brunswick's share increased from $13 million to $18.5 million.
Briefly speaking that is a summary of what New Brunswick received during the first three agreements. During the period of 1956 there was a series of conferences following which, for the first time, legislation was introduced entitled the tax sharing arrangements act instead of the tax rental agreements act. We all know the formula. It was 10-9-50 and New Brunswick's share averaged approximately $23.5 million. Very soon after the agreement came into effect a change of government took place in Canada and a dominion-provincial conference was held at Ottawa. I believe it was during the month of November, 1957. That conference was brought about as a result of strong criticism coming from the maritime provinces and Ontario with regard to the tax sharing arrangements act of
1957.	As a result, the formula was increased from 10-9-50 to a more generous level of 13-9-50. At that time agreement was also reached in principle on a special grant to the Atlantic provinces. As a result the tax sharing arrangements act was amended in 1958 in order to provide for an additional sum in round figures, of $100 million over a four year period to the four provinces in eastern Canada. As a result of the amendments in
1958,	New Brunswick's share-and I may say
[Mr. Deschatelets.l

I have been using New Brunswick figures throughout-increased from the questionably generous offer of the previous administration of $22.5 million to a figure in 1958 of $31.6 million or an increase of nearly $10 million which figure has continually increased during the years 1959 and 1960. Consequently I think it is very difficult, and indeed impossible, for Liberal speakers to try to convince anybody living in the Atlantic provinces that the formula and equalization basis introduced by the former St. Laurent administration was in any way at all fair or acceptable to the poorer provinces.
In fact, if one looks at the tables introduced by the Minister of Finance on July 11 one notices-dealing again only with New Brunswick-that in 1956-57 under unconditional grants that province received approximately $19 million and an additional $8.7 million under conditional grants, or a total payment in the year 1956-57 of less than $30 million. In the current year, instead of receiving less than $30 million the province of New Brunswick is receiving in excess of $60 million. This small province increased its source of revenue as a result of the change of administration to the extent of 100 per cent or, in round figures, from $30 million to $60 million annually.

speechtext:
A pretty substantial
increase.

maintopic: AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
That is an increase of $5 million, as opposed to an increase of $30 million.

Most of the criticism from the Atlantic provinces comes from one source, the premier of New Brunswick. He has raised public objection to this new scheme. He calls it discriminatory, suggesting that it is against the interests of the poorer provinces. In order to strengthen Premier Robichaud's argument he complains about the large stuns going to be paid to the provinces of Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland. In other words, he is suggesting that these three other provinces in eastern Canada are not poor provinces; that New Brunswick is the only poor province in eastern Canada.
To strengthen his argument further he has recently endorsed the former policy of the Progressive Conservative government of New Brunswick in reference to the division of the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants. In Hansard last week a telegram was tabled from the premier of New Brunswick addressed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker). That telegram appears at page 8769 of Hansard of September 22 and reads as follows:
New Brunswick favours thirty-thirty-thirty-ten distribution of Atlantic provinces grant.
In other words, in one moment he criticizes part of the formula and the next moment completely endorses the distribution agreed to by the premiers of the four provinces in the year 1958. The main objection from New Brunswick seems to be that the new formula includes 50 per cent of provincial revenue from natural resources in the equalization formula. Yet it is a known fact that revenue from this source in the case of New Brunswick is substantially well below the national average. Therefore New Brunswick's share will be a larger percentage under the new equalization formula than if this provincial revenue were excluded from the formula. It is included to make certain that more fiscal aid will be given to the less prosperous provinces rather than the reverse under the formula introduced by the Liberal administration.
The province of New Brunswick has also complained, alleging that it objects to the inclusion of the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants in the equalization formula. These grants are not included and are separate and distinct according to the bill. In fact the Prime Minister assured Premier Robi-chaud of that policy in recent correspondence, particularly in a letter dated August 30 which was tabled in the house. The Prime Minister was dealing with the subject of the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants and the alleged inclusion of these grants in the equalization formula. I should like to quote one short paragraph from this recent letter:
Dominion-Provincial Relations
You refer at a number of points in your letter to the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants and contend that these grants should be kept separate from the other fiscal arrangements. In fact, the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants will continue to be a separate grant and the increase of $10 million in the total amount will benefit your province to the extent of $3 millisn per annum, which is the 30 per cent share of the additional grant of $10 million. This grant will be paid separately and is in no way connected with the basic equalization formula which ensures that New Brunswick will receive an equalization payment sufficient to raise revenues from the standard taxes and 50 per cent of the natural resource revenues to the per capita national average yield.
These grants are not a part of the equalization formula in any way, shape or form. Admittedly they are part of the guarantee formula. However, if one searches the records he will find that in the past under former agreements New Brunswick did not qualify or receive any benefit under the stabilization principle. It is my hope and the hope I believe of most people in New Brunswick who have an interest in its welfare, that at no time in the future will this province or any other province in Canada have to rely on the guarantee provisions. In fact, it is the hope of all concerned, premiers, politicians and interested citizens that none of the provinces in Canada will have to rely on the guarantee provisions.
In any case, the guarantee principle in no way hurts New Brunswick and the equalization formula contemplated in this bill is, if anything, in favour of all provinces which are in a less fortunate financial situation. In my opinion the objections raised by the premier of New Brunswick are hardly warranted. When the formula under the new bill is increased to the level of 20-9-50, which it will reach in the last year of the five-year agreement, New Brunswick stands to gain an additional $3 million approximately. This means that each and every year between 1962 and 1966 as the formula goes from 16 to 20 per cent in reference to personal income tax collections, this province, and every province in Canada, can expect its income to increase. It appears to me as though the province of New Brunswick, in a desperate move, is criticizing this bill in order that it may blame someone else for its own faulty administration. Perhaps it is trying to get sufficient additional money from Ottawa to carry out in full its election promises of 1960.

On March 27, 1957, the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) was the guest of honour at Athens at the most important political meeting which was ever held in that village in Leeds county. The meeting place was filled to capacity and the hon. gentleman made a profound impression on the people who listened to the address, indeed some listened from outside the hall. There were two points which the hon. member for Eglinton pressed on the citizenry of that community. The first was that it was inconceivable that a government with a half billion dollar surplus should continue in this fashion and make so few tax cuts. The other point was that the provinces and in particular the municipalities in Ontario were in a critical position financially and that their situation had to be drastically remedied. This, he said, would come about if the people placed their confidence in a Conservative administration.
A few days after this there was a meeting on May 3, 1957 when the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) said the municipalities were being pauperised while the federal government wallowed in surpluses the like of which have not been seen in Canadian history.

May I give the comparative figures, the mill rates for three typical towns or villages in the area-Brockville, Gananoque and Smiths Falls. At the time the minister was speaking the mill rate for residents in Brockville was 63.5; today, it is 76. The industrial rate then was 69.5; it is now 81. I read to the committee of this house last night a headline indicating that the municipality of Brockville was gravely concerned as to how it was going to meet its record relief payments. I pointed out that the situation was critical and I asked the committee to remember some of the undertakings to Ontario, which appears from everything we have heard to be one of the privileged parts of Canada. At a political meeting in Toronto on the evening of March 19, 1958, Premier Frost, introducing the present Prime Minister, said:
I have talked of $100 million. I am convinced as I never was before that we are going to produce a new deal.

May I read to the house the concluding sentence of an editorial which appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail on June 5. It is called "The Crumbs from the Table", and reads:

I cannot, of course, stop this gloomy Cassandra from prophesying as he pleases, but it seems to me that past experience should prompt the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont to ask him-himself what would be the reaction of the people of this country should as tragic an event as the one he has just forecast become a reality. While listening to his complaints about the present situation and the blame he was putting on the Conservative government with regard to this tax-sharing issue, I was casting my mind back on all the events which, since 1939, have marked Canadian politics and shaken the very foundations of our constitution. Naturally, I connect those events with the presence of a Liberal government at the head of the country. That is why I find it difficult to believe the remarks made in this house by all Liberal members, and that is why I found it difficult to credit with sincerity a political party which was, for so many years, the contented promoter of constitutional disintegration.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make one or two very short remarks on the general problem involved in the bill before us.
First of all, I should like to remind hon. members of a fact which I feel is basic, and that is that the stand of the members from Quebec on the problem involved in this bill cannot necessarily be the same as that of the members from the other provinces. I will probably surprise nobody by repeating, after a great many leaders, that the province of Quebec is not a province like the others and that, for this very reason, it cannot take the same stand as the other provinces on certain issues. Quebec has to consider carefully and circumspectly all constitutional proposals, for these proposals often

contain important factors for the future of the people who make up the majority in the province of Quebec.
I am not an expert on constitutional matters, far from it, Mr. Speaker. Therefore, I could not pretend to be well informed nor go into technical details on the various solutions which can be brought to our constitutional problems. However, having studied very recent history, that is the history of the last 15 years, I realize that a change has come about since 1958 which leads us to believe-and I am one of those who believe it-that our constitutional problems are being given a solution more in line with the general principles of our Canadian constitution.
A moment ago, the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont referred to the so-called autonomist spirit which is typical of the Liberal party. subtopic: PROPOSED DECLARATION ON DISARMAMENT

speechtext:
September 22, 1961
The following is submitted by the United States of America as a proposed declaration on disarmament for consideration by the general assembly of the United Nations as a guide for the negotiation of a program for general and complete disarmament in a peaceful world.
Declaration on Disarmament:
A Program for General and Complete Disarmament in a Peaceful World
The nations of the world,
Conscious of the crisis in human history produced by the revolutionary development of modern weapons within a world divided by serious ideological differences;
Determined to save present and succeeding generations from the scourge of war and the dangers and burdens of the arms race and to create conditions in which all peoples can strive freely and peacefully to fulfil their basic aspirations;
Declare their goal to be: A free, secure, and peaceful world of independent states adhering to common standards of justice and international conduct and subjecting the use of force to the rule of law; a world where adjustment to change takes place in accordance with the principles of the United Nations; a world where there shall be a permanent state of general and complete disarmament under effective international control and where the resources of nations shall be devoted to man's material, cultural, and spiritual advance;
Set forth as the objectives of a program of general and complete disarmament in a peaceful world:
(a)	The disbanding of all national armed forces and the prohibition of their re-establishment in any form whatsoever other than those required to preserve internal order and for contributions to a United Nations peace force;
(b)	The elimination from national arsenals of all armaments, including all weapons of mass destruction and the means for their delivery, other than those required for a United Nations peace force and for maintaining internal order;
(c)	The establishment and effective operation of an international disarmament organization within the framework of the United Nations to ensure compliance at all times with all disarmament obligations;
(d)	The institution of effective means for the enforcement of international agreements, for the settlement of disputes, and for the maintenance of peace in accordance with the principles of the United Nations.
Call on the negotiating states:
(a)	To develop the outline program set forth below into an agreed plan for general and complete disarmament and to continue their efforts without interruption until the whole program has been achieved;
(b)	To this end to seek to attain the widest possible area of agreement at the earliest possible date;
(c)	Also to seek without prejudice to progress on the disarmament program agreement on those immediate measures that could contribute to the common security of nations and that could facilitate and form a part of that program.
Affirm that disarmament negotiations should be guided by the following principles:
(a)	Disarmament shall take place as rapidly as possible until it is completed in stages containing balanced, phased and safeguarded measures, with each measure and stage to be carried out in an agreed period of time.
(b)	Compliance with all disarmament obligations shall be effectively verified from their entry into force. Verification arrangements shall be instituted progressively and in such a manner as to verify not only that agreed limitations or reductions take place but also that retained armed forces and armaments do not exceed agreed levels at any stage.
(c)	Disarmament shall take place in a manner that will not affect adversely the security of any state, whether or not a party to an international agreement or treaty.
(d)	As states relinquish their arms, the United Nations shall be progressively strengthened in order to improve its capacity to assure international security and the peaceful settlement of differences as well as to facilitate the development of international cooperation in common tasks for the benefit of mankind.

(e)	Transition from one stage of disarmament to the next shall take place as soon as all the measures in the preceding stage have been carried out and effective verification is continuing and as soon as the arrangements that have been agreed to be necessary for the next stage have been instituted.
Agree upon the following outline program for achieving general and complete disarmament:
Stage I
A.	To establish an international disarmament organization:
(a)	An international disarmament organisation (IDO) shall be established within the framework of the United Nations upon entry into force of the agreement. Its functions shall be expanded progressively as required for the effective verification of the disarmament program.
(b)	The IDO shall have: (1) a general conference of all the parties; (2) a commission consisting of representatives of all the major powers as permanent members and certain other states on a rotating basis; and (3) an administrator who will administer the organization subject to the direction of the commission and who will have the authority, staff, and finances adequate to assure effective impartial implementation of the functions of the organization.
(c)	The IDO shall: (1) ensure compliance with the obligations undertaken by verifying the execution of measures agreed upon; (2) assist the states in developing the details of agreed further verification and disarmament measures; (3) provide for the establishment of such bodies as may be necessary for working out the details of further measures provided for in the program and for such other expert study groups as may be required to give continuous study to the problems of disarmament; (4) receive reports on the progress of disarmament and verification arrangements and determine the transition from one stage to the next.
B.	To reduce armed forces and armaments:
(a)	Force levels shall be limited to 2.1 million each for the U.S. and U.S.S.R. and to appropriate levels not exceeding 2.1 million each for all other militarily significant states. Reductions to the agreed levels will proceed by equitable, proportionate, and verified steps.
(b)	Levels of armaments of prescribed types shall be reduced by equitable and balanced steps. The reductions shall be accomplished by transfers of armaments to depots supervised by the IDO. When, at specified periods during the stage I reduction process, the states party to the agreement have agreed that the armaments and armed
forces are at prescribed levels, the armaments in depots shall be destroyed or converted to peaceful uses.
(c)	The production of agreed types of armaments shall be limited.
(d)	A chemical, biological, radiological (CBR) experts commission shall be established within the IDO for the purpose of examining and reporting on the feasibility and means for accomplishing verifiable reduction and eventual elimination of CBR weapons stockpiles and the halting of their production.
C.	To contain and reduce the nuclear
threat:
(a)	States that have not acceded to a treaty effectively prohibiting the testing of nuclear weapons shall do so.
(b)	The production of fissionable materials for use in weapons shall be stopped.
(c)	Upon the cessation of production of fissionable materials for use in weapons, agreed initial quantities of fissionable materials from past production shall be transferred to non-weapons purposes.
(d)	Any fissionable materials transferred between countries for peaceful uses of nuclear energy shall be subject to appropriate safeguards to be developed in agreement with the IAEA.
(e)	States owning nuclear weapons shall not relinquish control of such weapons to any nation not owning them and shall not transmit to any such nation the information or material necessary for their manufacture. States not owning nuclear weapons shall not manufacture such weapons, attempt to obtain control of such weapons belonging to other states, or seek or receive information or materials necessary to their manufacture.
(f)	A nuclear experts commission consisting of representatives of the nuclear states shall be established within the IDO for the purpose of examining and reporting on the feasibility and means for accomplishing the verified reduction and eventual elimination of nuclear weapons stockpiles.
D.	To reduce strategic nuclear weapons
delivery vehicles:
(a)	Strategic nuclear weapons delivery vehicles in specified categories and agreed types of weapons designed to counter such vehicles shall be reduced to agreed levels by equitable and balanced steps. The reduction shall be accomplished in each step by transfers to depots supervised by the IDO of vehicles that are in excess of levels agreed upon for each step. At specified period during the Stage I reduction process, the vehicles that have been placed under supervision of the IDO shall be destroyed or converted to peaceful uses.

(b)	Production of agreed categories of strategic nuclear weapons delivery vehicles and agreed types of weapons designed to counter such vehicles shall be discontinued or limited.
(c)	Testing of agreed categories of strategic nuclear weapons delivery vehicles and agreed types of weapons designed to counter such vehicles shall be limited or halted.
E.	To promote the peaceful uses of outer
space:
(a)	The placing into orbit or stationing in outer space of weapons capable of producing mass destruction shall be prohibited.
(b)	States shall give advance notification to participating states and to the IDO of launchings of space vehicles and missiles, together with the track of the vehicle.
F.	To reduce the risks of war by accident,
miscalculation, and surprise attack:
(a)	States shall give advance notification to the participating states and to the IDO of major military movements and manoeuvres, on a scale as may be agreed, which might give rise to misinterpretation or cause alarm and induce counter-measures. The notification shall include the geographic areas to be used and the nature, scale and time span of the event.
(b)	There shall be established observation posts at such locations as major ports, railway centres, motor highways, and air bases to report on concentrations and movements of military forces.
(c)	There shall also be established such additional inspection arrangements to reduce the danger of surprise attack as may be agreed.
(d)	An international commission shall be established immediately within the IDO to examine and make recommendations on the possibility of further measures to reduce the risks of nuclear war by accident, miscalculation, or failure of communication.
G.	To keep the peace:
(a)	States shall reaffirm their obligations under the UN Charter to refrain from the threat or use of any type of armed force- including nuclear, conventional, or CBR- contrary to the principles of the UN Charter.
(b)	States shall agree to refrain from indirect aggression and subversion against any country.
(c)	States shall use all appropriate processes for the peaceful settlement of disputes and shall seek within the United Nations further arrangements for the peaceful settlement of international disputes and for the codification and progressive development of international law.
(d)	States shall develop arrangements in stage I for the establishment in stage II of a UN peace force.
(e)	A UN peace observation group shall be staffed with a standing cadre of observers who could be dispatched to investigate any situation which might constitute a threat to or breach of the peace.
Stage II
A.	International disarmament organization:
The powers and responsibilities of the IDO shall be progressively enlarged in order to give it the capabilities to verify the measures undertaken in stage II.
B.	To further reduce armed forces and armaments:
(a)	Levels of forces for the U.S., U.S.S.R., and other militarily significant states shall be further reduced by substantial amounts to agreed levels in equitable and balanced steps.
(b)	Levels of armaments of prescribed types shall be further reduced by equitable and balanced steps. The reduction shall be accomplished by transfers of armaments to depots supervised by the IDO. When, at specified periods during the stage II reduction process, the parties have agreed that the armaments and armed forces are at prescribed levels, the armaments in depots shall be destroyed or converted to peaceful uses.
(c)	There shall be further agreed restrictions on the production of armaments.
(d)	Agreed military bases and facilities wherever they are located shall be dismantled or converted to peaceful uses.
(e)	Depending upon the findings of the experts commission on CBR weapons, the production of CBR weapons shall be halted, existing stocks progressively reduced, and the resulting excess quantities destroyed or converted to peaceful uses.
C.	To further reduce the nuclear threat:
Stocks of nuclear weapons shall be progressively reduced to the minimum levels which can be agreed upon as a result of the findings of the nuclear experts commission; the resulting excess of fissionable material shall be transferred to peaceful purposes.
D.	To further reduce strategic nuclear weapons delivery vehicles:
Further reductions in the stocks of strategic nuclear weapons delivery vehicles and agreed types of weapons designed to counter such vehicles shall be carried out in accordance with the procedure outlined in stage I.

E.	To keep the peace:
During stage II, states shall develop further the peace-keeping processes of the United Nations, to the end that the United Nations can effectively in stage III deter or suppress any threat or use of force in violation of the purposes and principles of the United Nations:
(a)	States shall agree upon strengthening the structure, authority, and operation of the United Nations so as to assure that the United Nations will be able effectively to protect states against threats to or breaches of the peace.
(b)	The UN peace force shall be established and progressively strengthened.
(c)	States shall also agree upon further improvements and developments in rules of international conduct and in processes for peaceful settlement of disputes and differences.
Stage III
By the time stage II has been completed, the confidence produced through a verified disarmament program, the acceptance of rules of peaceful international behavior, and the development of strengthened international peace-keeping processes within the framework of the UN should have reached a point where the states of the world can move forward to stage III. In stage III progressive
controlled disarmament and continuously developing principles and procedures of international law would proceed to a point where no state would have the military power to challenge the progressively strengthened UN peace force and all international disputes would be settled according to the agreed principles of international conduct.
The progressive steps to be taken during the final phase of the disarmament program would be directed toward the attainment of a world in which:
(a)	States would retain only those forces, non-nuclear armaments, and establishments required for the purpose of maintaining internal order; they would also support and provide agreed manpower for a UN peace force.
(b)	A UN peace force, equipped with agreed types and quantities of armaments, would be fully functioning.
(c)	The manufacture of armaments would be prohibited except for those of agreed types and quantities, to be used by the UN peace force and those required to maintain internal order. All other armaments would be destroyed or converted to peaceful purposes.
(d)	The peace keeping capabilities of the United Nations would be sufficiently strong and the obligations of all states under such arrangements sufficiently far reaching as to assure peace and the just settlement of differences in a disarmed world.
